subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON STATEMENT OF MR. PEARSON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not often that I have the opportunity to congratulate a minister, not only upon his speech but also upon the policy he

enunciates. I find myself in substantial agreement with what the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) said yesterday. As the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) pointed out, our support may be embarrassing; nevertheless it is a fact. I have had the opportunity of visiting Lake Success on several occasions during the past few years. It has been most gratifying to realize the high position which Canada has among the nations of the world. It is attributable, of course, in no small measure to the efforts of Canadians themselves during the last ten years, to the high calibre of our civil servants abroad and to the present minister himself. Indeed I regard his appointment to the important position of chairman of the political committee of the assembly as a personal tribute to him as well as a tribute to Canada.
I should like to express my gratitude for the courtesy and co-operation I have always received from members of his department, and for the information which has always been so willingly given when asked for. Yesterday the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) said he felt there was not enough publicity about our policies. That may be so, but I do not think the fault is entirely that of the department. Perhaps part of the fault lies with the Canadian daily newspapers, which give a regrettably small space to foreign affairs. This is something the Canadian Daily Newspapers Association might look into, rather than the minister. I have always received information when I asked for it. Sometimes it has been given in confidence, which I hope I have never violated any more than I have violated confidences in respect to information received in personal conversations with a minister.
Yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs pointed out the successes the United Nations organization had achieved- partial successes, it is true-in Kashmir, Palestine and Indonesia, and we have to give the organization credit for those. Indeed it is obvious that had the United Nations not existed, we should have had to create it. But there was also the most significant failure of all-the failure of the organization to provide the security which the nations feel they need. If this failure was not met with the hopelessness and cynicism which followed the failures of the league of nations, perhaps the league did not die in vain. But today I think it is much more generally understood that the problem of international government, which has defied the wit of man through the centuries, cannot be solved merely by drawing up paper constitutions. However, since the United Nations could not provide us with the security we felt we required, it was

obviously the responsibility of government and of parliament to take measures to provide it in other ways, under the aegis of the United Nations organization. This we hope we have achieved through the North Atlantic treaty. We hope it will provide a measure of security which is not provided in any other way.
Yet while I agree completely with what the minister said yesterday about article 2 of the treaty, I cannot but underline what the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) said as to the economic bases for peace. On occasions I have found the hon. member for Vancouver East to be wrong; but I have also found that when he and I agree on something, there is very little room left for argument. Article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty deals with international economic co-operation, while article 9 deals with the immediate establishment of a defence committee. A careful reading of the communique tabled in this house by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) on September 19, following the first meeting of the ministers of external affairs of the various countries signatory to the treaty, indicates that this question of economic co-operation was given but scant recognition. In paragraph VIII the communique states:
The council recognizes the importance of economic and financial factors in the development and1 implementation of military plans for the defence of the north Atlantic area.
That is certainly putting the cart before the horse, because if as the result of an economic collapse our allies in western Europe become bankrupt, there will be no military security whatever. Indeed our military security will be enhanced by the improvement of the economic conditions of those countries. I hope, therefore, that the minister will constantly endeavour to bring before the members of this group the tremendous importance of economic co-operation and collaboration, so that we may all play our part with the knowledge that we are strong economically as well as in a military sense.
Obviously the problem which obsesses the world is Russia. Members rose in this house yesterday and expressed their fear of communism. This fear, which we all share, is something that we as democratic socialists have known about for a long time, for we have no illusions about communism or communist parties. But the answer is not to be found by people standing up here or on other platforms, tearing their hair and rending their garments and offering no alternative. There has to be an alternative to communism if we are to survive. The alternative might be rather expensive, but I know of no other.
External Affairs
Communism breeds on hunger, on poverty, and on racialism. Just a few weeks ago the Prime Minister of India spoke in this chamber. When I heard Liberals and Conservatives, along with the rest of us, applaud, and quite rightly, that great world figure, the situation seemed to me to be ironical. I could not rid my mind of the thought that if Mr. Nehru had been a citizen of British Columbia three years ago these same Liberals and Conservatives, because of the colour of his skin, would not have seen fit to give him the vote. Now the wheel has turned with a vengeance, and I am glad of it. Mr. Nehru said in part, at page 1104 of Hansard:
There is another facet of this Asian situation to which reference must be made. The so-called revolt of Asia is a striving of the legitimate pride of ancient peoples against the arrogance of certain western nations. Racial discrimination is still in evidence in some countries, and there is still not enough realization of the importance of Asia in the councils of the world.
I do not think-at least I would rather not think-that those remarks were addressed to us in Canada. They may have been directed to another member of the commonwealth of nations-South Africa, where today the administration is carrying out a policy toward the native population which can only give aid and comfort to communist movements all through Asia. The racialism we see there is every bit as bad as that which existed in Hitler's reich, and every bit as dangerous. South Africa cannot plead that this is South Africa's business only; for questions which were once solely domestic affairs now concern the whole world and the safety of all. And it is quite conceivable that the attitude of Asia as a whole may be conditioned by what happens in the Union of South Africa. Already the coloured population have powerful champions, and I hope we in Canada will number ourselves among them.
On the same occasion Mr. Nehru spoke of the dire poverty which afflicted so many thousands, indeed millions, of the people of Asia. This dire poverty is a situation we have to face up to. Yesterday there was much reference to Christianity, and the fight between atheistic materialism and Christianity in this world; but the Christian faith can survive only when it can deliver the goods; when it can show that we mean business; when we can say that we are prepared to practise what we preach-and that is what we may find to be expensive. Anything which has been expended on the Marshall plan is but a drop in the bucket compared with what will have to be spent from now on. If we say that we adhere to the Christian faith, we have to accept its implications, the implication that there is the
1872

External Affairs
fatherhood of God, and therefore a brotherhood amongst man-and the natives of Asia are as much our brothers as anyone else.
The practical application of this belief means that if we have surpluses which we cannot use after our own people are looked after, and after we have sold what we can, rather than destroy them , we have to be prepared to give them away. It will pay us handsomely to be in a position to help alleviate the starvation in Asia and in other areas of the world. It will be expensive. There is only one way in which we can do it, and that is by taxing our own people. Already there are indications that we are going back to the situation which existed in the thirties when, rather than give food away, we used to destroy it. Already this administration has subsidized the apple growers, paid them to uproot trees which could have borne fruit to be given to those who needed it. The philosophy is still there; the mentality is still there.
Nothing will please the communists more than to realize that the western nations are prepared to destroy food which starving millions need. I repeat that it will be an expensive proposition to live up to our responsibilities, but it is the surest way of defeating communism. Communism cannot be defeated by great armies; for bullets can never destroy ideas. If we can show people that we have a better way of life than the communists, then of necessity we shall emerge victorious.
Russia is working not only in the areas of the mind, but also in geographic areas. I am reminded that yesterday the member for Peel spoke of the lack of information about our foreign policy. Information is lacking not only about our current policies but about history as well. Sometimes we are the victims of our own lack of perspective. In Europe today we see the beginning of a union among certain nations. They are advancing a little, but perhaps in the light of history the advance has been great. There is still impatience, however, over here at the slowness of the progress in this direction. We have to remember that the problems of Europe are rooted in two thousand years of history, and we cannot expect them to act with the same celerity as we might on this continent. It is a lamentable fact, but true, that they might complete that integration rapidly as a result of aggression, and perhaps then this union would become almost immediately operative. But it would be too expensive a price to pay for it; so we must approach the problems of Europe with sympathy and with some understanding.
We need not fall into the error, which is ours as well as Europe's, of believing that Europe is still the centre of the universe,
EMr. Stewart (Winnipeg North).]
with the nations of the Far East on some dim and distant periphery. In deference to the Secretary of State for External Affairs I used that phrase "nations of the Far East" as a European colloquialism. Obviously the centre of affairs is shifting to the west. In this century the centre is going to be the North American continent. By the same token we must be ready to realize in years to come that the centre may move still farther west. We have to realize, too, that the rest of the world, perhaps the majority of the world, does not reason as we do. This in no way makes it inferior to us; but it is a fact which we have to face. Russia, India, Pakistan, China, and the other nations, look upon history quite differently from the way we do as a member of the western nations. They have not the same philosophy or the same attitude towards life, or indeed the same religion.
Some people in the United States-a minority, it is true-believed that a few years' military occupation of Japan would, in some mysterious way, change Japanese thinking. The statement of Premier Yoshida last week should rid them of that idea. One of our great tasks is to encourage the middle groups in many areas-the people who are struggling between reaction and communism. They are the groups known as democratic socialists. Last night the member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne) said that socialism is likely to lead to communism. I believe that is a misreading of history because wherever communism is indigenous it has sprung not from socialism but from black reaction such as we saw in countries like Russia before 1918. In those countries where democratic socialism is strong, communism is at its weakest. We have to be prepared to encourage every movement which will lead to any improvement in the standard of living and literacy of the peoples of the world.
We have to realize that in some countries such a position may mean revolution. We are mortally afraid of that word "revolution," although we are the products of it. Our parliament and our democratic processes, our conception of freedom, are the fruits of revolution carried on by our fathers in the past. The liberty we have today is the result of the revolt against tyranny in England, France, and the United States, so perhaps there is something to be said for revolution. There is much to be said for those groups who are trying to improve the conditions of the people and to remove oppression so that communism may be held in check. If that improvement can be achieved only by revolution, I do not think we should fear it as much as we say we do. Yet we

are faced with the fact that among the major western powers the principal support is for reaction, and that support, of course, means that they are playing directly into the hands of the communists.
Many of us on this continent, as well as in Europe, are completely unable to understand why the allied forces in Germany are approving the appointment of nazis to high positions in industry. There is the situation in Greece to which the minister referred yesterday, and I must admit that I do not share his optimism. For some years that country has been torn by strife and I fear will continue to be torn by strife for some time to some. There was a guerilla movement in Greece, in many ways completely legitimate. It was made up not only of communists but also of democratic socialists, such as myself, and Liberals such as those on the opposite side of this house. They had to flee to the mountains because of the persecution of a tyrannical government. It so happens that they were taken over by the communists and their grievances exploited by the Kremlin. In an attempt to rectify that situation, the United States has continued to pour money into Greece, perhaps $300 million a year, hoping for reforms which would hold communism in check. The only result we have seen of that vast expenditure is the continued greed and avarice of the Athens group which is still in power.
Every move that Russia has made in Greece has been carefully calculated, even to the betrayal of the guerillas. Betrayal is nothing new in Soviet Russia's history. Of this I am certain; even if the great powers of the world get out of Greece, there will still be a struggle between the dispossessed majority and a reactionary government. Our policy should be one of hands off. It is a policy which we might have to change, however, if other nations continue to interfere in what is happening in that country. I find it difficult to understand, let alone explain to others to whom we speak of our democratic faith, just why the great nations of the western world support reaction while they talk so glibly about democracy. I find it difficult to explain the inconsistencies in British and United States policies which accommodate themselves with great ease to the non-democratic institutions of countries such as Portugal, Turkey, the Arab nations, and conceivably yet, Yugoslavia. I feel that our government must have some policy in regard to that matter, because, if we are to take the minister's speech at its face value-and I think we are entitled to do so-these are not policies to which we can give support.
45781-119J
External Affairs
In this review yesterday the minister mentioned that communism was not making headway in Europe-in France, Italy, Finland, and I think he might also have mentioned Norway where, on October 10 last, the Labour government was once again returned to power with a greater majority. Not only was it returned to power, but the eleven communists who were members of the previous parliament were defeated. We should remember that the borders of Norway are contiguous to those of the Soviet union and the communists there were not eliminated by repression -which incidentally will never eliminate communism. They were eliminated because of the constructive measures of the government designed to improve the standards of living of the people. As we have said so often, this is the only way to combat communism.
There are other sore spots in the world. There is the Middle East, where even yet there is neither security nor peace, and I do not think there ever will be until the conflict over oil is stopped and the conditions of the Arabs materially improved. It is true-and I welcome it-that Israel is now recognized by the world. But unfortunately the neighbours of that country are still pawns in the game of power politics. In the Middle East the strategic importance of oil is paramount. Some nations feel it is a struggle for survival because oil is so important to the modern economy. But it is also a struggle by private groups for their own profit. There is only one answer that I can see. Again I may be accused of suggesting interference in the affairs of other nations, but I feel that the responsibility eventually will have to be assumed by the United Nations by its creating a trusteeship over the oil resources of the Middle East. That trusteeship should be used to protect the interests of the people who have been exploited for so many years by feudal rulers, and also to see that all countries are given free access to the oil which is there. The United Nations has a commission just now studying the economic conditions in the Middle East. What it will report I do not profess to know, but I hope that a trusteeship such as I have suggested will be one of the recommendations made. Of this much I am certain: if the situation in the Middle East is handled properly, this question of security may settle itself.
What about China? I think we might almost paraphrase the words of a certain statesman and say that it is a great country of which we know but little. I do not share the minister's modified eulogy of the regime which is vanishing. Indeed, I give it little credit. Whatever credit there is I reserve for those tens of thousands of Chinese peasants who

External Affairs
died helping to make our cause victorious. What we see today is a venal administration, clad in corruption, rapidly disappearing; and its place is being taken by a Chinese politburo.
The western nations did not realize the strength of the nationalism which existed in China. The Russians did, and they capitalized on that feeling in China, just as they are capitalizing on it in other areas; and of course they have designed it as far as they could for their own ends. While I may be unduly optimistic, I do not feel that Russian nationalism will in the long run prove a greater or more powerful force than the indigenous Chinese nationalism. China is not yet under the direct domination of the Soviet union; it may never be. But it is certain that many of its rulers have great sympathy with the ideas of the Kremlin. There are also some who cast an eye toward the west because they realize the tremendous need for western help. Who will survive, we cannot tell. The tip-off obviously will be when the purges start in China, as of necessity they must.
The great need for China is industrialization. Yet from the point of view of national resources, if one excludes Manchuria, it is not a rich country. As I said before, industrialization is impossible without help from the west. We can count on this. Russian influence will be used to the utmost to eliminate foreign markets, so that they may cripple us commercially still further; and Russian influence may be used to prevent the Chinese, or certain of them, from appealing to the west for the aid which they need if China is to become an industrial nation. It is much too early to decide what is going to happen. The situation is confused and in no small way bedevilled by the equally confused and vacillating policy followed recently by the United States which has been costly not only in terms of money but also in terms of prestige.
As to the recognition of China, I do not think anybody would be brave enough to say when that should take place. It is entirely a matter of timing. Recognition must take place obviously at the moment when too great prestige will not be given to the regime, and yet before it is too late for us to capitalize on that recognition.
In the debate on external affairs eighteen months ago I spoke at some length on the aims and aspirations of Russia. I gave my reasons then for believing that Russia was not ready for war. I see no reason for repeating them. But the real menace in Russia today, in my opinion, is not entirely the menace of what for want of a better word we call communism; it is Russian nationalism, which is a legacy from Ivan the Terrible down through Alexander the Great to the last of the IMr. Stewart (Winnipeg North).]
Romanovs. I am convinced that although the people of the Soviet union loathe the idea of war as much as we do, their leaders believe it to be inevitable. If that final tragedy of war should come, the atom bomb is going to be used and the results will be more appalling than any of us dares to contemplate. I agree therefore with General Romulo when he said in the assembly that "the means for controlling the destructive potentialities of this new force must be found", with the emphasis on the "must". This means that we must continue, with all the patience we have, to explore avenues of co-operation with the Soviet union. Mr. Vishinsky's hostile and insolent manner makes clear the tremendous difficulty there is of finding some common ground. Unquestionably, power must be on our side in a world of power politics. But in the long run that is not the best road to peace. Nevertheless, possession of adequate military power, and the additional moral power resulting from policies which are rooted firmly in our democratic and Christian traditions, may provide the time which is so necessary to break down the suspicion and the fear which besets the world. In the pursuit of that aim we Canadians have an increasingly important part to play.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON STATEMENT OF MR. PEARSON
speechtext:
first want to congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), who has returned to us after his heavy duties at Lake Success in connection with United Nations work. I want to compliment him on the brief though comprehensive resume that he gave of his work there. I am sure hon. members appreciate to the full the involved and intricate work that they have to do; and it will probably become more and more involved and more difficult as days go by.
In view of the fact that several references have been made to the Chinese situation, I felt that I should say something in that regard. As many hon. members know, I spent a little over two years with the United Nations relief and rehabilitation administration. Approximately two years of that time were spent in the China field. I have always been interested in this type of work. The first intimation I had of it was when Winston Churchill, that great wartime leader, said in the House of Commons in Great Britain in 1940, and through the House of Commons to the world at large, and particularly to the people of the nations who had been overrun by the Hitler forces and were held in subjection to them: "Hold on; do not give up. The allies will win the war, and when victory is achieved and the war is ended the United Nations will bring you food, clothing, relief and rehabilitation." He invited all other

nations of similar views to join with him in this very large project. Consequently, after some meetings and after a good deal of correspondence and publicity the members of the United Nations met in Atlantic City on November 3, 1943, and that is where the UNRRA agreement and the UNRRA charter were drawn up.
Nothing of its kind had ever been attempted in the world before. There was no precedent to go by. They had to venture out into a new field. They had to do something for these people. At that meeting they agreed that one per cent of the 1943 national income of these nations would be a fair basis on which to work. Representatives of many nations were there. Later others came in, until eventually thirty-three nations that had not been invaded and sixteen that had been invaded by the enemy during the war became members of the United Nations relief and rehabilitation administration.
The amount of money that was contributed to that organization was stupendous. It amounted to something over $3,500 million in United States funds. Of course the United States contributed much the larger amount, because they had much the larger income. Of the total they contributed something over seventy per cent. Great Britain was second and Canada was third. Canada's contribution was approximately $150 million. Of the total amount of money that was subscribed, the largest amount was earmarked for China. It amounted to $530 million. The total amount of supplies shipped in to China under this rehabilitation program approximated three million long tons. That in itself was a stupendous task.
As hon. members know, China is a very old country. It has a history which goes back at least six thousand years. It comprises almost one-quarter of the world's population. The population runs anywhere from 450 million to 500 million people. Therefore we must admit that that country is possessed of extraordinary powers of stamina and resistance. After all these years, and in spite of famine, flood, disease and war, both foreign and civil, they comprise one-quarter of the world's population.
I was in that country almost two years doing UNRRA work. It would be presumptuous on my part to say that I know much about their problems, because a country with a civilization that old and steeped in tradition after all these years has problems that could not be solved by a foreigner going into that country and staying such a short time. A noted war correspondent, and later a press correspondent, was once asked to
External Affairs
write the bottom facts of China. He replied that there was no bottom and there were no facts.
I was assigned to the department of investigation and inspection, to see that the supplies that were sent into China were channelled through their proper courses and went to the places to which they were allotted and assigned, and to see also that they did not get sidetracked and on the black market. That in itself was quite a problem. It was a stupendous task because the transportation system of China was totally inadequate to handle that amount of supplies, and it had been further disrupted by the war.
In this capacity I visited many parts of China. I was intensely interested in seeing that these supplies did go to the place to which they were allotted and that the people did get the maximum amount of relief. I was also interested in the standard of living of the people, and in the type of government they had. I also wanted to find out, if I could, what had kept that vast body of people in such a primitive state as they had been all through these centuries.
I found that China was a country of approximately four million square miles in area. It has an area larger by one-third than that of the United States. It has thirty-four provinces, with a governor over each province, including, of course, Manchuria.
In the ordinary course of events the UNRRA supplies that were distributed in Europe were distributed through the municipal offices, the Red Cross organizations and other government agencies, but in China that was not possible. Therefore a different procedure was followed in China. The Chinese national government set up an organization of their own called CNRRA. They set up approximately the same kind of organization as UNRRA, and we dealt through the CNRRA organization. Fifteen regional offices were set up in places which had been devastated and war ravaged by the Japanese invasion. The problem was to distribute these supplies in the proper places. That was the first time that I had some slight differences with the CNRRA organization, whose function it was to see that these goods and supplies were distributed properly. Under the terms of the agreement with the UNRRA organization these supplies were to be distributed without discrimination as to race, creed, or political differences in the war ravaged and war devastated areas. The CNRRA organization was at times reluctant to send the supplies to the communist held territories, which after all had been devastated and ravaged the same as the others. With that in mind I worked in China. I must confess that I went to China

External Affairs
wholly convinced that the national government, which was headed by Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, was the government that should be reinstated and supported by other nations. After I was there a while I wondered whether that was true. I began gradually to change my mind, and often used to think of the Shakespearian play, Hamlet, where Polonius was saying farewell to Laertes and, not expecting to see him again, gave him this as his farewell warning:
Neither a borrower nor a lender be;
For loan oft loses both itself and friend,
And borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry: This above all: to thine own self be true,
And it must follow, as the night the day.
Thou canst not then be false to any man.
With this in mind I tried to draw my own conclusions as to the exact problem in China, or as to what was the solution, if there was any. I did as the late General Stilwell did; I wrote my own diary, and wrote it carefully from day to day. I do not expect I shall ever publish it, but if it is published it will show what I saw from day to day.
During the week end I reviewed my diary to be sure that I had it correct. I will say that I could not believe such poverty could have existed-such privation, such hardship, such misery. I could not believe that such want prevailed anywhere in the world in the year of our Lord 1946, the first year I was in China.
Even the great city of Shanghai, the greatest metropolis in China, with many modern buildings-even in that great city the poverty was indescribable. It beggared description. According to their own census, they would pick up each morning the corpses of forty or fifty people who had passed away in the preceding twenty-four hours.
Another condition which brought about great misery was inflation. When I went to China in 1946, through the medium of brokerage offices and exchange shops one could buy United States dollars and gold bars. One could buy the British pound, but most of the business was based upon United States dollars. When I went there, one United States dollar would buy 1,200 Chinese dollars. The Chinese currency became more and more depreciated until it reached the point of 200,000 to one. When I left China late in 1947 the exchange rate was 500,000 Chinese dollars for one United States dollar.
This meant great privation for the people, because the price of rice was greatly inflated. People were not able to buy, because they did not have enough of their own devalued money. It became so bad that in many places shops were closed and commodities were not sold. In some places people would pay for meals when they went into restaur-

ants for fear the prices of the meals would go up before the meals had been eaten. The merchants raised or marked up the prices of their goods many times, even three times in one day. All this caused misery and hardship; it resulted in much suffering among the common people of the country.
I have kept in fairly close touch with China since my return. About a year after I came back the exchange rate stood at about eight and one-half to nine million for one United States dollar.
I found that illiteracy in China was prevalent to the extent of at least eighty per cent. I believe it is a fact that eighty per cent of the people in that great country are illiterate-able neither to read nor to write. They had no schools to go to, and no teachers to teach them. This fact in itself added greatly to the difficulties we experienced in supplying the people with the food and clothing, relief and rehabilitation contributed by the United Nations.
It must be kept in mind of course that the Japanese began their invasion of China as early as 1931, and gradually took over the country. They first took over Manchuria, and by 1945 nearly one-half of the total country was in their hands. UNRRA was the greatest humanitarian plan ever devised by the mind of man; there can be no question about it. To my mind it was a preliminary Marshall plan; it was a stopgap. It was merely to stop people going to the left in large numbers and forming themselves into bandits who would have entirely disrupted the country. It was a plan to bring people back to a normal way of living.
I was pleased of course to be associated with that humanitarian organization, one with such a fine background. We know some mistakes were made. It is true, yes, that some of the cotton sent over in 1946 by UNRRA to be used for the relief of the Chinese people never reached the people. In the main, however, it did. I believe there were something like 550,000 bales of cotton sent. It is true that some of that cotton reached the cotton mills, and some was used to make uniforms for the armed forces. It is true that about 20 million feet of lumber, the finest that could be purchased from California to British Columbia, was not used for the purpose for which it was intended, namely, the rehabilitation of the fishing industry. It is true that some of the food did reach the army.
All this was inevitable. But in the main the organization did succeed in what it set out to do, and many millions of lives were saved. Much hardship, suffering and privation was alleviated by the distribution of

supplies and the work done by UNRRA in the Chinese field. Let me say that the people of China did know where those goods came from and, in the main, were most thankful. They did appreciate the services and the supplies given by the United Nations.
Because of war some of China's potential production was lost. For instance, in 1935 she produced enough cotton for her own industry-something in the neighbourhood of two million bales. That supply, however, was pretty well dissipated and destroyed during the war. UNRRA brought over many tons of better types of cottonseed, types which would produce longer staple. This was distributed among the cotton farmers-in itself a worth-while contribution.
Many hundreds of tons of vegetable seeds were brought over, with the result that they were able to produce a much better type of vegetable, and were in a position to produce their own seed. I am convinced that China could increase her production by one-third if a proper system of fertilization were introduced and improvements were made in the types of seeds and in farm cultivation.
Another worth-while form of aid took place during the war of 1939, when a portion of the dikes of the Yellow river were blown out, with the idea of stopping the progress of the Japanese forces. This was an attempt to flood out the Japanese, and to drown them; but not many of them were drowned. In the Yellow river basin more than two million acres of the best fertile land were flooded and kept out of cultivation. One of the things UNRRA did-and it was a stupendous engineering task-was to rebuild those dikes so that the river might be returned to its former course and two million acres of fertile land brought back into cultivation to relieve the suffering and the hunger of the Chinese people.
A first-class job was done by UNRRA in connection with displaced persons. This organization undertook to bring back to their former homes people who had been displaced during the war. When the Japanese came, they carried away many of the Chinese to the inland areas to be used in the building of bridges and roads, thus virtually making slaves of them. These displaced persons had no means of returning to their homes; therefore UNRRA undertook to provide transportation, food and shelter during the period of rehabilitation.
In 1946 I visited some of these refugee camps where UNRRA was supplying temporary shelter, food and clothing to help the people return to their homes. I went with some of these refugees when they were being returned to their homes in Honkew, people
External Affairs
who had been separated from their families for several years. In most instances what they went back to was only a hovel, a mass of rubble; but they picked out pieces of their own furniture, took their bamboo poles and started to rebuild their mud houses with straw-thatched roofs. The re-establishment of these people in their homes was a most worth-while project.
I think the IRO took over the displaced persons program in April, 1947, and they have been carrying on since then. During the days of UNRRA operations, there were 800,000 displaced persons who had to be brought back to their former homes. UNRRA also undertook to transport Europeans who had been caught there during the war back to their own lands. When IRO took over in April, 1947, there were still some 11,300 Europeans waiting to be transported to their homes. Many of them were probably hard cores who could never go back, but a great many of them did, and have by now been transported to their own countries. There were also many thousands of Chinese still to be returned to their homes.
I knew Mr. Jennings Wong, the director of IRO, very well. He was a most capable Chinese, and I worked with him during the fisheries rehabilitation program. A year ago he asked me to go back to China and help him with the IRO program. He knew of my attitude to the then Chinese government, and was appreciative of it; we talked about it many times. In view of the situation in China, and the expectation I had of conditions becoming rapidly worse and worse, I sent him a cable and told him I could not go.
While a part of the rehabilitation project has not been completed, by and large the UNRRA program was a worth-while contribution, and did much to relieve the suffering, hardship and privation of the Chinese people. That is something that will never be lost, because it will be remembered for many years. The Chinese are a very friendly people. We made many friends among them, and they will not forget the work we did.
It seemed to me that the background of the Chinese people was that one dynasty would rule year after year until it became so weak and corrupt in its court life that another dynasty would overthrow it and come into power. The last dynasty that held power in China was the Manchu. It carried on until October 10, 1911, when that young revolutionist, Dr. Sun Yat-sen, upset the Manchu dynasty and set up his so-called republic. Since that time the 10th day of October has been celebrated as a national holiday and is called "double tenth day". There is national

External Affairs
patriotism, but a national viewpoint seems to be lacking when personal interests are at stake. In 1925 Dr. Sun Yat-sen was in Peking negotiating a peace treaty with the so-called communists of that day in order to establish a national government, but he took ill and died. In 1947 I visited Peking again. Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek came into power after Sun Yat-sen died, and he was president of the republic until a short time ago.
I remember visiting Peking in July, 1947, and I had lunch at the great Waggon Lee hotel there. I saw on the bulletin board that there was to be a Rotary dinner that day, and I went in and found they had a large club. Seventy-five per cent of the members were Chinese, and the remaining twenty-five per cent were foreigners like myself. The speaker of the day was Mr. Wells, a New York Times correspondent from Tientsin, and his subject was the economic crisis there. He spoke in English, because the ceremonies were practically all conducted in that language. He told us of the graft and corruption in the operations of the nationalist government in the city of Tientsin. In conversation with him afterwards he told me about conditions that to me were unbelievable. I could not believe that they could exist anywhere in the world.
While I know nothing about the personal integrity of Chiang Kai-shek, I understand from his friends that it is quite good; nevertheless I know that his government officials practised a policy of graft and corruption that was incredible to me. I have also visited many cities of China and met many merchants. I met Colonel Kearney, of the United States army, who was stationed there. He told me about many things that happened in the Chinese army which to me were inconceivable. When I went to China I understood that it was one of the great democracies of the world. According to my understanding and appraisal of democracy, it was as far removed from the principles and doctrine of democracy as it possibly could be. I could not conceive of conditions being as bad as they were. To me it was capitalism at its worst, where a few people controlled the whole policy and the rest lived in poverty and privation.
In my opinion Russia is capitalism in reverse; the people of Russia have lost their liberties and rights through a system of state socialism or communism. In both Russia and China it seems to me that the people are helpless pawns in the hands of their rulers. When I returned home in 1948 I told people not only in Washington but in Canada many times that I did not see how the then Chinese government could possibly win the
[Mr. Mackenzie (Lambton-Kent).J
war. That was the opinion I had formed after exhaustive investigations. I visited the merchants in many cities of China, men who had been Chinese merchants for years, and I asked them about the situation. They told me that they could not continue, that there would have to be a change, because they could not go on under present conditions. When I came home I suggested that the only way to achieve peace and unity in China was to follow a middle-of-the-road course.
When secretary of state George Marshall visited China in 1946, on several occasions he endeavoured to get the fighting forces together, and he almost accomplished it. I met many people connected with student bodies and democratic leagues, and I used one of the best interpreters available in order to try to get at the real cause of existing conditions. I found there was practically no support among the better thinking people for the government then in power.
What will the situation be under the present regime? That is something we probably cannot foresee. When I saw so much trouble, so much privation, and such terrible conditions, I said to myself many times: How can you support a government which condones, approves and contributes to a policy of feudalism, oppression, graft and corruption? How, in the name of democracy, liberty and Christianity, can you support such an outfit anywhere in the world? I could not do so. I do not know what will happen in the United Nations if the present regime in China should be recognized by Canada. It is two years since I visited China, and probably conditions have entirely changed. Many of the people I met in China were not pro-Russian, but antiRussian. They were afraid of the Russian regime, but they could not continue under the old set-up. If that is the condition today, as I am firmly convinced it was two years ago, then if you want to maintain some stability -and I believe there is some stability now- I believe the new regime should be recognized as soon as possible. If that is not done, the result will be to drive these people into the open arms of Russia, which I think would be disastrous. This is something, of course, the United Nations will have to take into consideration. I think I saw in this morning's newspaper that Mr. Bevin was going to consult with the other nations about recognition of the new government in China.
When I was in China, associated with this great international body, it had a personnel of about two thousand, most of whom were from the United States. Others, however, came from all over the world-from South Africa, from India, from Egypt and other countries. Most of them could speak a little

English. It was what we call pigeon English, but at least we could understand each other and could carry on correspondence. Invariably they would ask me: "What state do you come from?" When I told them I did not come from a state, that I came from Canada, without exception they replied, "We think that is a wonderful country to live in. We think it is the best place in the world. Unfortunately your immigration restrictions will not permit us to go there, but we would like to go." I am fully convinced that no country stands in as high regard among the nations of the world as Canada does today; and this is something of which we should be very proud.
Many factors have contributed to Canada's position in this regard-the stand Canada has taken at international conferences, where we have always adopted the middle-of-the-road course; the fact that we have no territorial ambitions of our own, and that we have always stood for the rights of the common people. I must confess that I had to leave the shores of Canada and go to a foreign land before I fully appreciated what this country should mean to us and what this country has to offer. I believe we have a better standard of living, greater security and a brighter future than any other country in the world. I believe we have the best form of government, and I think we should support it. It is true that we have not solved all our problems; but as long as the world lasts you will never get a government that functions one hundred per cent. If we want to halt communism; if we want to make sure that communism finds no place here, let us teach Canada to the children in the schools and the young people in our universities. Let them compare this country with Russia and her satellites, and I am sure they will appreciate that Canada really is the best country in the world.
Then when the revolutionary days are over-and they will be over-we will need all our intelligence to adapt ourselves to the conditions of the new era. I am quite sure I do not need to tell the minister that it will be a matter of compromise and co-operation- though you cannot compromise too much. I mean that there must be a certain amount of give and take, but it cannot be all give or all take. We should never give up hope, however, as long as we can keep the nations of the world around the conference table, as long as we can maintain some kind of co-operation. You will remember that the league of nations failed because one country after another left it and refused to co-operate. Then we had two separate groups of countries that strengthened themselves in preparation for war; and no doubt that is what we would see if the United Nations should fail. I repeat that
External Affairs
if we are to have peace in the world-and we must have it-it will have to be a matter of co-operation and compromise.
Many times I thought, when reading the late Wendell Willkie's book "One World", that if he had lived in China or India for any considerable period he would have realized that one world would not be possible in our time, but it probably will come much closer to realization in the life of this generation. In the United Nations we have racial divisions, we have differences of creed, we have economic conflict. But we have all those problems here in this country in some degree. The United Nations can draw up a basis of agreement, to be sure, but beyond that it is up to the individual people. We must support the United Nations, and must support its policies; for they touch the lives of all of us. Unless we live those policies in our hearts and souls and minds, unless we support that organization completely, it can never be a success.
In conclusion I urge that we make it our aim and ambition so to live, so to strive and so to serve and work that we shall be able to play our part in creating a better understanding among the races of the world and making a contribution toward the raising of the standards of living of those poor unfortunate people who are unable to help themselves without help from the European and western powers.
Let me close my remarks with a proverb I learned in China. It was written in Chinese, but I had it translated; and it went like this:
Where there is righteousness in the heart, there Is beauty of character. Where there is beauty of character, there is harmony in the home. Where there is harmony in the home, there is order in the nation; and where there is order in the nation, there is peace in the world.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON STATEMENT OF MR. PEARSON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the course of this debate yesterday and today my mind has kept turning back to a scene in a third-year classroom at the university of Toronto some twenty-six years ago, when a young professor arrived to deliver his first lecture. He was very young; in fact he looked as though he might be an undergraduate himself. He spoke with a slight lisp; but he quickly commanded the attention of his students and, in a very short time, won their complete affection. I had the good fortune to be a member of that class; and the young professor who came to deliver his first lecture, in English constitutional history, was one Lester B. Pearson, who soon became known to all undergraduates as Mike. Little did I think then that he and I would today be sitting on opposite sides of this house participating in a debate of this nature.

External Affairs
li he will permit me-because I must still treat him with the deference that a former student must ever show to his professor-I should like to compliment and congratulate him on the admirable speech he made yesterday, in which he gave such a comprehensive review of our external relations. One thing I admired about it, in addition to its comprehensiveness, was that it was realistic and did not pull any punches, especially when dealing with the Kremlin menace which overhangs great sections of the world today. I thought it was refreshing to hear from the lips of the Canadian Secretary of State for External Affairs plain, bold truths, spoken without mincing words. It seems to me that is a refreshing and encouraging note in discussion of our international relations.
This debate, sir, is timely. I am one of those who feel that this parliament should have more frequent debates on external affairs. If we are to do our duty to those who sent us here, it is necessary to see that the Canadian people are provided with essential information concerning world affairs, so that great developments may not take place unknown to them, or cataclysmic and startling events burst upon them without warning. Such debate is necessary, too, so that the beneficial effect of public opinion may be felt in this chamber and in that way exerted upon those who are responsible for administering Canadian external policy.
Yesterday the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) said something I do not intend to repeat but wish to concur in completely. He laid great emphasis upon the necessity for discussion in this house and for provision of the fullest information as to the developments in our external relations. A good example of that is the interesting speech which has just been delivered by the member for Lamb-ton-Kent (Mr. MacKenzie). It brings to our minds this fact, sir, that our interest in the great events that are taking place in distant areas of the globe is not merely an academic interest. We listened closely to the hon. member's account of events in China, not as something remote from us, but, apart from the fact that he spoke from personal experience, as relating to events, unfolding themselves in China today, which have a direct bearing upon our life and our future in Canada.
As this world shrinks, and as Canada grows in strength and importance, so our horizons as citizens of Canada must broaden. This will be possible only if parliament does its share in shaping the thought of Canadians.
Mention has been made, sir, of the fact that in essence we have in Canada-I shall not say a nonpartisan foreign policy, but certainly a bi-, or tri-, or quadri-partisan foreign

policy. It is revealed in the speeches which have been delivered in this debate. It seems to me that has been one of the elements of strength in Canada's external relations in these eventful post-war years. The fact that the two principal parties at least have seen substantially eye to eye in matters affecting Canada's external policies has been a contributing factor of great significance in the rising importance attached to Canada's voice, and her position in relation to the other nations of the world. I hope that condition may continue. I feel it is the duty of every member of the house to strive to make it possible for our foreign policy to be continued on that level and not be drawn into the area of partisan conflict. This will be possible if between the government and the house-and when I say "house" I mean all parties in the house-there exist mutual confidence and a disposition on the part of the government to be thoroughly frank with the house on these subjects at all times.
With this thought in mind, I should like to echo what my colleague the member for Peel said yesterday in urging the government to make a clear statement as to the extent to which the government may have gone in any particular in committing itself in the conferences that have been proceeding in recent months following recent international treaties and agreements.
We are actually debating, sir, a motion to refer certain of the estimates, namely the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, to the standing committee on external affairs. I believe this procedure is worthy of comment, in view of one or two remarks that were made yesterday.
As one who has sat on that committee since it was first established in 1945, I wish to commend the procedure that the house is asked to approve. Not only has that procedure been beneficial in past sessions, but it has provided a vehicle serving two useful purposes. First, it has enabled the members of this house sitting on that committee to elicit more detailed information about the operation of the Department of External Affairs and the way in which government policy in relation to foreign affairs works itself out through that department than would be possible in the house. In the second place, it affords an opportunity for a more efficient review of the estimates and expenditures.
These two worthy purposes have been well served under the procedure that has been followed with respect to the estimates of this department. We welcome the opportunity for accounting furnished by this motion, and urge that the example be followed by ministers ol other departments in relation to other standing committees of the house.

My principal reason for speaking in this debate today is to lay before the members of the house some conclusions reached and some observations made largely in the course of my travels in Britain and on the continent of Europe a year ago. Since that time there has not been a debate in the house which would provide an opportunity for discussing some of the observations made on that tour, which in itself was a very interesting experience. With some other hon. members of this house, it was my good fortune to be one of the Canadian delegates to the commonwealth parliamentary conference which assembled in London in October, 1948. It afforded to the delegates an opportunity to meet some exceedingly interesting people in England, Scotland and Northern Ireland, and representatives from all parts of the commonwealth and the empire. After the conclusion of the conference, it was my good fortune to visit Greece, Italy, France, Belgium, The Netherlands, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Germany, and Ireland, which at that time was still Eire. I do not pretend, sir, that that tour makes me an authority on this subject. If, however, the house will bear with me, I should like to share some of the experiences and some of the observations made in the course of that eventful tour.
In the first place, one cannot undertake a tour of that kind, coming in close contact, as I had the opportunity of doing, with Canada's representatives abroad-when I say "representatives" I mean not only those of ambassadorial or ministerial rank but the staffs in the embassies and legations-without a feeling of pride and satisfaction in the realization that the diplomatic side of the public service has attracted to it so many able men. I wish to speak now particularly of the younger men. This department had the good fortune to enlist the services of a large number of young men who came out of the armed services at the conclusion of the war. They are men with a good education, a clear mind and, in many cases, I believe they have a bright future before them. That has been one of the great advantages that Canada has enjoyed, because it has given vigour and clarity to our relations in the capitals of other nations. I hope that as time passes these younger men will be given encouragement, and will from time to time be appointed to leading positions in the diplomatic services as men who have earned those positions by right of promotion and by long service. I do not say that every ambassadorial post must be filled by a career diplomat, but I hope that as time goes on the young men who have been brought into the public service
External Affairs
in this field, and who have had the opportunity of developing, will not be denied the opportunity of reaching the higher posts in the diplomatic service of Canada.
I should like to say, too, that visits from Canadians, particularly those in public life, to some of the more distant countries I have mentioned, would be good for our representatives there and for those who have the good fortune to visit those countries. Particularly in the three Scandinavian countries that I visited I was told that few members of the Canadian parliament are ever seen there. May I say this to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I hope he will encourage his able deputy to visit as many as possible of these diplomatic posts abroad if he cannot do it himself. Firsthand contact will be extremely useful on both sides. It will be possible in that way to understand some of the immediate problems that men in the diplomatic service abroad, in all ranks, are facing. There are many acute difficulties as a result of exchange problems in these recent times.
One cannot visit Britain without a thrill of pride when one sees that, submitted as it was to the severest test that any nation in all history has ever undergone, it came through in such way as to fulfil the prophecy of Winston Churchill: so long as the world shall last, though the nation shall last a thousand years, men will say that that was Britain's finest hour. It is with sadness that one sees today the heavy price that that nation is still paying for her tremendous exertions and her almost unlimited sacrifices during the war.
As the minister has said, the commonwealth today can boast of increased achievements. Within the past year and a half we have seen the addition of three young partners to the list of the members of this British commonwealth of nations. They are old countries, but young members of this commonwealth. It was the great privilege of those of us who were delegates to the commonwealth parliamentary conference to come in close contact with the delegates from these new dominions. They were a most interesting study. The Indian delegation, for instance, was a strong one. In fact, one can say that about all those delegations. Nearly every one of them-and there was one woman among them-had a record of imprisonment sometimes aggregating a long period of years. Yet there was not in the conversation of one of them-and to me this was a most agreeable fact-the slightest trace of bitterness toward Britain. This surprised me, and I made it my business to ask some of these Indian delegates the reason. The answer was: It is due to Gandhi, because Gandhi always insisted that we were not

External Affairs
fighting Britain; that we were fighting against what we considered to be the imperialistic system, and Gandhi always insisted that there should be no bitterness.
It is an amazing fact, Mr. Speaker, that today those who are leading India into the new paths of self-government upon which she has entered are men whose minds, notwithstanding their experiences of the past, are, with hardly any exception, free from bitterness arising out of their past experiences. Their whole attitude could be summed up in this way: We thank Britain for this gift of self-government; we are determined to show Britain and the other nations of the world that we deserve this gift, and that we are going to make good. The same may be said of the delegates of Pakistan and Ceylon, although they have not had the experiences I have mentioned in relation to most of the Indian delegates.
In the light of events elsewhere in Asia, particularly in China, and events that may soon make themselves felt in the smaller countries south of China, it is of the greatest importance, not only to Canada but to the whole civilized world, that we should see rising on this subcontinent of India a nation dedicated to peace and to democracy, and representing the principal hope of the world today for the maintenance of stability in the Far East. There was a time when many people of the western world regarded China, because of her long record of faithful attachment to peace, as the hope of the future in Asia. But having regard to events that are occurring in China today, the thoughts of the world are being transferred to India as the principal basis for the hopes that we build of peace, stability and democracy in the Far East. We may be thankful for the vitality of democracy in that land, and the vitality of the belief in democracy that is shared by Mr. Nehru and the other Indian leaders who are following him so faithfully in their tasks.
Looking at what is happening there, is it not a thousand pities that Burma was so hasty in her decision, in view of what she might have been saved in the light of the decisions made at the prime ministers' conference in April last? She might have had everything she sought in the way of sovereignty and yet have continued to enjoy the benefits of membership in this great commonwealth.
Yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs mentioned with regret the departure of Ireland from the commonwealth. I am sure it is a matter of the most profound regret to all Canadians that the government and the Dail of Ireland have not seen their way clear to remain as a sister nation in the

commonwealth. I simply make this observation on that departure. While in Dublin it was my good fortune to discuss this matter with the Prime Minister, Mr. Costello. I had the opportunity of meeting individually all the members of his cabinet, as well as Mr. de Valera, the leader of the opposition. The reasons that were given by the government for the course which it had then announced, and which became effective within a short time afterwards, do not reflect any ill will, either toward Britain or toward other nations in the commonwealth.
Mr. Costello said two things. He believed, first, that the step that was being taken would be a contribution toward better relations with Britain. In the second place, he said that it would remove, as a source of political strife, the question of relations with Britain, which had been exploited in times past by politicians there as a means of advancing their political interests. Just as we in Canada, to our great loss, have had racial and other differences basely exploited for political purposes, so in Ireland differences with Britain have been exploited for political purposes. We can only hope that there will continue to prevail that measure of good will which was professed by all the leaders of that country at the time they took their fateful step.
Europe is a fascinating study at any time; and I do not think one could have visited the countries in Europe I have mentioned at a time when a more interesting study would have been possible. Of the importance of recovery in Europe, particularly in western Europe, both politically and economically- and I may say spiritually as well-there can be no question. If the world is to tread the paths of peace and to be delivered from the uneasy mood under which it has laboured since the war, then Europe must undergo that restoration, political, economic and spiritual.
There are two bright rays of hope in the European scene. One is the fact that in some of the countries statesmen of great stature have arisen who are giving leadership to their people. In the second place, United States aid, both in the material sense in the way of money and in leadership, has been invaluable. No Canadian ever ought to underestimate the contribution that the United States has been making to the restoration of Europe and the preservation of democracy in western Europe.
One thinks, of course, of France because of its leading position. One thinks of conditions a year ago, when strikes and riots, precipitated by the communists, were being

aimed at the breakdown of government in that country-diabolical attempts which that nation has survived. France now seems to be moving into smoother paths, although she still faces formidable economic difficulties.
Belgium came through the war and entered the post-war period with her economy probably in better condition than that of any other nation involved in the war. The Netherlands suffered terribly during the war, and one of the great difficulties in working out a customs union between Belgium, The Netherlands and Luxembourg has been the great disparity between economic conditions in Belgium on the one hand and in The Netherlands on the other. Progress has been made, and the good feeling among those nations augurs well for the future.
As to Italy, several of us Canadians who were there at the time had the opportunity of conferring with the Prime Minister, Mr. de Gasperi, and members of the Italian government. Italy has had a heavy struggle against tremendous economic and political difficulties. By those of us who may be prone to think of Italy principally in terms of her role as an enemy country in the earlier years of the war, and of the treachery and the perfidy that accompanied Italy's entry into the war under the hand of that villain Mussolini, this fact should be remembered: Italy today is led by a man who is a great democrat. Mr. de Gasperi was in exile throughout the twenty years of Mussolini's regime. He found exile in the Vatican; otherwise undoubtedly he would have ended his days in a concentration camp. After twenty years of exile in the Vatican throughout Mussolini's regime, he returned and is today taking a prominent place among the statesmen of Europe in leading his country forward. Italy has a tremendous population problem. There are two million unemployed in that country. That is the essence of Italy's great economic difficulty.
Mention has already been made in this house, and I do not need to dwell upon it, of the way in which the tide of communism has receded in Europe, in all the countries that I have mentioned, and also in the Scandinavian countries. In moving through the Scandinavian countries one was conscious of the fact that the communists are losing ground. Naturally I made it my business to try to find the reason. Everywhere I went I found from those with whom I talked- people in public life, members of the press and citizens-that the factor that made the impression upon those countries, which were countries attached to the democratic way of life, the thing that had opened their eyes to
External Affairs
the reality of communist aims in Europe, was what happened in Czechoslovakia. It was all very well for them to shrug their shoulders at what happened in Poland, in Roumania, in Bulgaria, in Hungary and in Albania, because those countries seemed to be far away, and all of them had not had the record of wholesome attachment to democratic ideals that had prevailed among the brave Czechoslovakian people. What happened in Czechoslovakia? The communists found their way into the government under the guise of colleagues, under the guise of coalition. They quickly grasped the key posts of power in the government. Then when the time was ripe, and acting on instructions from the Kremlin, they seized power. There cannot be any compromise between democracy and communism. Events in Czechoslovakia have proven forever that democrats and communists cannot work together in the same government. The events in Czechoslovakia contributed mightily to the opening of the eyes of the peoples in the democratic nations in western Europe, and not least of all in the Scandinavian countries. What has happened in elections that have occurred there since is simply the culmination of a process that was quite evident at the time.
A year ago today I was in Berlin. It was an amazing experience to be in that city of ruin. But probably more impressive than the ruin was the airlift. The airlift is not simply a closed chapter of history. The political significance of the airlift should not be underestimated by those who are shaping events in the world scene, and who are looking forward to what may happen in the days to come. It was a marvel of organization; it was a tremendous triumph of the western nations, Britain and the United States, over Russia in the cold war. I do not stop now to examine the technical features of it. It fell to the good fortune of a member of the other place, Senator Moraud, and myself to see this airlift in actual operation, to fly in on it to Berlin and out on it, to see it in operation, both at Gatow airport, which was used by the Royal Air Force, and at Tempelhof airport, used by the United States air force. On both fields freight planes were landing and taking off every three minutes. An aeroplane was taking off or landing every one and a half minutes, and all of them were controlled by one man in the control tower. It was our good fortune to be in that control tower, and to see this whole operation laid out before us. It was a costly operation, but it was successful.
There are those who say that a great mistake was made by the leaders of the allied powers during the war in planning for the

. External Affairs
joint occupation of Berlin. Well, sir, whether a mistake was made or not-and I for one am not convinced that a mistake was made- the fact of the matter is that, once joint occupation was decided upon, its continuance was essential; it was necessary that the western nations, which Russia was trying to push out of Berlin, should stand their ground. A decision of the most vital and far-reaching importance was taken in concert by Great Britain and the United States when they decided that they would stand their ground in the face of tremendous pressure exerted upon them by the Russians, deliberately exerted to force them out, and thus to cause loss of prestige to the western nations in eastern and middle Europe, and also to snuff out the flicker of hope still entertained by the peoples in those countries that some day they might live to recover their freedom; and to show them that their hopes were in vain.
It was a triumph of unity between Great Britain and the United States. Not only did it preserve their position in Berlin; not only did it preserve the hopes of those who were outside the iron curtain that the western powers were still strong enough to stand up to pressure from Russia, but it has served to keep alive behind the iron curtain the hope of those unfortunate, unhappy people that the day will come when they will recover their freedom.
That triumph of the airlift has been responsible, to a greater extent than has been recognized, for the fact that it became possible to enlarge the scope of the Brussels pact into the North Atlantic treaty. I think the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) will bear me out when I say that the strong stand of Great Britain and the United States, their show not only of strength but of will to stand up to the Russians in that situation, was largely responsible for creating in the minds of the smaller nations of western Europe a willingness to enter into military commitments with the stronger nations and to make this North Atlantic pact an effective and comprehensive instrument of policy on the part of the democratic nations to restrain further Russian aggression in Europe.
May I digress to say that I hope, before he closes the debate, the Secretary of State for External Affairs will say something further to the house about whatever efforts are being made to pursue the drafting of the peace treaties with Germany and Austria.
One is conscious of the tremendous difficulties. One is conscious of the fact that the western nations must certainly keep alive a loyalty to the cause of democracy, and the

support that democratic leaders in Germany enjoy from the people of Germany today.
I am not commenting on just how deep that loyalty is, or how quickly it may be lost; but I am sure that those who are responsible for directing the external policies of the western nations are alive to the necessity of strengthening the hands of the democratic leaders in Germany today. I had the opportunity of talking to some of these democratic leaders in Berlin, and learning the feelings they harbour as to the uncertainties facing them if their hands are not strengthened.
In the very few moments remaining to me I should like to say something about Greece. All too little is known in the western world about what has been happening in Greece. If more were known, less would be said on the part of some to the effect that what has occurred in Greece since the war has been merely a civil war. I spent some days in Greece-not simply in Athens? but also up in the battlefields of the north. We were taken to Janina; there we were within view of the battleground of the Grammos mountains where a very important battle had been fought against the guerrillas in April, 1948.
What has happened in Greece has not been a civil war. It is true that large numbers of the guerrillas were Greeks; but that was no cold war: that was a hot, shooting war, and that force of guerrillas had foreign help behind them. Russian planes were supplying the guerrillas who were fighting in large numbers in the difficult mountain areas of Greece. It was the communist countries to the north of Greece- Yugoslavia, Bulgaria and Albania-which were harbouring those guerrilla forces, supplying them with bases and hospitals, and seeing that they were armed with everything they needed to make their incursions into Greece from those bases.
Their methods were the typical communist methods-diabolical in the extreme. When they raided the villages they shot the men who would not consent to being conscripted into the guerrilla ranks. Their homes were destroyed, and their children were abducted by the thousands and carried over the border to the communist countries to the north. When I was in Paris-where, I may say, I was treated with the greatest kindness by the Secretary of State for External Affairs- while the United Nations assembly and the political committee of which the minister is this year's distinguished chairman were in session, I heard the Yugoslav delegate complaining in the strongest terms against the action of Mr. Trygve Lie, the Secretary General, who had banned the showing, under

United Nations auspices, of a film which, the delegate said, showed the conditions under which Greek children were being reared in the schools of Yugoslavia.
Those children had been taken from their homes, from their parents in Greece, by these communist raiders, and carried across the border to the communist countries in the north. They were to be reared there and filled with communist hatred and communist doctrine until they were old enough to bear arms. Then they were to be sent back to join the guerrilla forces for the purpose of overthrowing the lawfully constituted government of Greece.
I wish to say something about democracy in Greece. If free discussion in the parliament of a country, the utmost freedom on the part of an opposition to attack and to criticize the government, is a true badge of democracy, then there is democracy in Greece today. Half a dozen of us Canadians were accorded a reception in the parliament of Greece, something for which we must always be thankful. We saw there with our own eyes the kind of debate that was taking place. I can tell you that there was no pulling of punches on the part of opposition members in that house. There we saw democracy working in an elected chamber, just as it works in this chamber, with the utmost freedom on the part of members of the opposition to speak and to criticize.
Greece holds a most strategic position in the world today. If Greece had fallen behind the iron curtain, the whole balance of power in the world would have changed, throwing the eastern Mediterranean under the power of Russia in that vital area where Russian policy has been trying to advance Russian influence for the last two hundred years.
The brave people of Greece have suffered great privations. Their attitude is one of profound gratitude to our nation for the gifts of wheat and other supplies from this country, through the Red Cross, and the Aid-to-Greece fund operating with the Allied War Relief fund. These gifts actually rescued that whole nation from the verge of starvation, because when the Germans moved out they took everything with them. They took all the medical supplies; they took all the food. They denuded the hospitals and other institutions of healing in the same way.
It filled us Canadians who were there with pride, to receive on every hand an unrestrained expression of gratitude from the Greek people to Canada for what this country has done. There is no more grateful people in the world than the people of Greece. It filled us with pride to see the Greek people standing on the streets of Athens and cheering when
External Affairs
the car of the Canadian ambassador drove by flying the Canadian red ensign. General LaFleche has done great work there. He has been a very popular figure in Greece.
