I hope we shall hear in this chamber no word of criticism-although I thought the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) came very close to it today-I hope we shall hear no word of criticism of American aid to Greece, because it was that American aid that has made it possible for the Greek people to expel these diabolical communist guerrillas from their midst, and give the people the chance, which they have been denied from the time war burst upon them in 1940, to rebuild their country and walk in the paths of peace. A great task of reconstruction awaits the Greek people who have suffered so much, and have earned our admiration and our gratitude for holding fast the gateway to the west against the invaders from the east.
Then, sir, this is my final word: whatever may be found disappointing in the international situation; whatever may be the misgivings of some in view of our disappointments, particularly in the security council of the United Nations, failure, should it come, must never be the result of any defection on our part from these institutions or the ideals they represent. The obligations we have undertaken are sacred to us. No matter what others may do to dishonour their obligations, ours must remain inviolate.
As we survey the uneasy present and the dark past I think we can all take fresh heart when we remember that there is committed to us as one of the western nations the cause of freedom, the cause of the dignity of man, the cause of honour and fair dealing among nations.
At one o'clock the house took recess.
The house resumed at three o'clock.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON STATEMENT OF MR. PEARSON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that every hon. member of the house is grateful indeed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) for the clear, frank, comprehensive and informative survey, which he gave us yesterday morning, of conditions as they exist today in this troubled world. It was a sombre statement. There was not much ground for optimism, certainly none for overoptimism, but there were rays of hope and encouragement here and there, for which we are all thankful. I think also that in the course of giving his review the Secretary of State for External Affairs impressed each of us with the fact that the conduct of the external relations of Canada rests in very capable and

External Affairs
understanding hands. Lastly, I am sure that we were all impressed, as we listened to him reviewing world affairs, with the tremendous responsibility which he carries as the responsible minister, and which this government or any other government carries in the field of international relations today.
In rising to make a few remarks-incidentally, the first which I have made-I do not propose to try to resurvey world affairs or even to deal with questions of high policy. I should like to undertake a much more humble task. I should like to speak for a short time about the Department of External Affairs itself because I believe it is a department of vital importance and concern to our whole future, and that its history has contributed a good deal to the development of our nationhood.
I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) that the work of the department is not as well known as it should be, but I cannot agree with him as to the reasons. If I understood him correctly, I think he attributed the situation to a lack of education and publicity on the part of the government, and to some sort of attitude that possibly the department had a selfappointed aloofness. I do not think either of these reasons is correct. I do not think either of them is the reason why the department is not adequately known, appraised and appreciated.
In my opinion there are two reasons for this condition. In the first place I think a specific interest in external affairs on the part of every individual is hard to establish and maintain except in relation to the broadest terms of policy. After all, every man has his duties and responsibilities, and he is quick enough to appreciate anything the government does that affects him. If taxes are raised you do not have to worry about publicity; but if somebody propounds that the Secretary of State for External Affairs possibly is not taking the right position in regard to something that happened a month ago in Pakistan I do not think people become greatly enthused about it. We tend to leave these matters in the hands of the government. We tend to leave consideration of these matters to others because we cannot hope to keep up day by day with the facts on which judgment must be based.
Second, I think the Department of External Affairs must, almost of necessity, be a somewhat silent department. It is an advisory department; it collects facts and information and advises the ministerial heads of the government. Its service to Canada is an indirect one. I do not think it can be put in the same position as, for example, the Department of

Public Works and the Post Office Department, which touch on tangible things that concern most members of parliament, and probably most people throughout the country. Nevertheless I believe that the department is doing an outstandingly good job.
I should like to point out that the work of the department and of its responsible heads day by day is most exacting. They must deal with a multitude of varied and complex questions which must of necessity be dealt with promptly and effectively, and frequently without any clear idea ascertainable at the time as to what the ultimate effect may be, because in foreign affairs the world is never static. It is changing every day, and the department and its responsible heads must keep abreast of every development and try to interpret it. Therefore it seems to me that the actions of the responsible heads of the Department of External Affairs must be the responsibility of the government which has to be judged and approved in the final analysis. I think that is true of other countries. I do not think therefore that the government or the department is open to criticism of any kind as to that phase of the matter.
The Department of External Affairs goes back a long way. It originated out of confusion because each department of the government was writing its own letters to different departments of other governments in the world. Sir Joseph Pope, who was under-secretary of state at the time, and who had been Sir John A. Macdonald's private secretary, in order to bring order out of confusion suggested that some department should be created to handle such matters, and he prepared a memorandum of which I shall read only a couple of sentences. It seems almost quaint now in the light of what has happened since that time. This is what he said in 1907:
I recommend that a small staff of young men, well educated and carefully selected, be attached to the department which I have advocated, and that they be specially trained in the knowledge and treatment of these subjects. In this way we shall acquire an organized method of dealing with international questions which at present we wholly lack.
Two years later, in 1909, forty years ago, that recommendation was followed and the Department of External Affairs was created. It was then a mere adjunct of the Department of the Secretary of State. It had a small staff consisting of one deputy minister, two chief clerks and four clerks. It was little more than a channel of external communication, but soon after it was formed it was attached to the Prime Minister's office and he became Secretary of State for External Affairs. In this particular I do agree with the hon. member for Peel that we might well

find a less unwieldy title. The department continued growing steadily until 1946, when a separate portfolio was created which was assumed by our present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). He continued in that portfolio until 1948, when the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) was appointed.
In the meantime the department has grown from its inception in 1909, until now we have over 170 highly trained and specialized technical officers, and a staff of over 800, operating through twenty-three embassies and legations, seven high commissioners, numerous other special representatives, and many consular offices.
I should like to pause for a moment to pay tribute to the under-secretaries who have made this great development possible. Because he was a close friend of mine, first of all I should like to pay tribute to the late Dr. Skelton, a very able, self-effacing and industrious man, who literally worked himself to death in the service of this country. He was succeeded by Mr. Norman Robertson who, as we all know, has represented us as high commissioner in Great Britain, then by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs, and finally by Mr. Arnold Heeney, whom we all know. I wish to pay tribute to these men for the work they have done. I think Mr. Mackenzie King should be regarded as the father of this department whose estimates are now before us, since he was in charge of its development during the formative years.
Prior to world war II these estimates were not very large, amounting to perhaps six, seven or eight hundred thousand dollars a year. Today, leaving out the extraordinary expenditures, they amount to about ten million dollars, or about one-half of one per cent of the total estimates of the country.
For a moment or two I should like to examine what we get in return for this expenditure. Perhaps we could put it in this way, that such expenditure is supplementary to our vast expenditures for national defence, which I suppose we must regard as the cost of our police force. These estimates, it seems to me, might well be called an insurance premium against the risk of war; and, like all insurance premiums, they carry no guarantee. However, it is the best we can do and offers the best protection open to us. It enables us to pool our risk of war with the other nations of the free world in what we might call an international Lloyd's and I think it gives Canada an outstanding opportunity, as events have proved, to work in the interests of peace and security, which are the keystones of our policy.
External Affairs
It enables this government, representing this country, to contribute effectively and continuously to the diplomatic effort now being put forward-the cold war, if you like, in which we are desperately engaged-in the hope that we may later avoid a shooting war in which we and all the other peoples of the world might perish. This is a bitter struggle; the stakes are great, and I do not think any other department of government bears the heavy responsibility that is carried by the Department of External Affairs.
The greatest field of its activities, of course, is within the United Nations organization. We all realize, with some sadness, that that organization has not fulfilled to any major degree the high hopes held when it was formed; but our hopes still live, and we dare not let them die. Yesterday I was pleased when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) said he believed-and he should be in the best position to know- that the United Nations had strengthened rather than weakened during the past year. That is a heartening and encouraging statement.
Now let us look for a moment at the contribution made by this government, working through the Department of External Affairs, to the work of the United Nations. In the formulation of the charter at San Francisco; in the deliberations of that organization year after year; on the atomic energy committee; on the security council; on the economic and social council; and now through our chairmanship of the political committee, this country has made a contribution second to none and in my opinion far greater than that of any country in the world at all comparable with us in either size or population. In passing I should like to observe, and I believe all hon. members will agree, that the election of our Secretary of State for External Affairs to the chairmanship of the political committee was no accident. It was a tribute to this government and this country, and a personal tribute to the great qualities of the man himself.
A number of specific phases have been mentioned in which this country has given active leadership; but for a moment I should like to deal with only one; that is, the drawing up of the North Atlantic pact. Who contributed to the success of that effort more than or even as much as our present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent)? No man gave more of his effort in the early days of the United Nations in an endeavour to establish the rule of law throughout the world than our Prime Minister; and when he saw that was going to be impossible of attainment at least within the appreciable future he threw his

External Affairs
energies, and this time with success, into the formation of what we call the North Atlantic pact, to provide collective security in this area. This was a new departure; it broke new ground in international affairs, and in itself was a practical step forward which may lead to other steps should the United Nations fail in its over-all objectives.
I had the privilege of attending one of the assemblies of the league of nations as secretary of the Canadian delegation. That was a place where I could never find in authority anyone whose thoughts matched the realities. It was a very pleasant, platitudinous place, but they did not tackle serious, practical problems. Whether it succeeds in whole or in part the United Nations has moved one step forward, because no one can accuse it of being platitudinous; no one can accuse it of not facing up to the problems. I think the North Atlantic pact may yet stand as one of the great contributions made within the organization of the United Nations; and with that contribution our own country, through the efforts of the present Prime Minister, has been closely associated.
There is another point about the North Atlantic pact I should like to emphasize. It is not merely a military alliance, which was the old method of entering into mutual defence pacts. It provides also for complete economic co-operation. About a year ago the Prime Minister put it in these words:
We must get clearly Into our minds the fact that a security treaty will not be fully effective if it is nothing more than a military alliance. In order to create and maintain an overwhelming preponderance we must have on our side not only military strength but also economic and moral strength.
That represents to me, Mr. Speaker, the highest order of international statesmanship, because it marks a new step forward in the close association of the free nations of the world. It was accentuated yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, when he said:
We must bring about the widest possible economic collaboration at the earliest possible date.
So I say this government is certainly taking its full part, and more, in the strenuous battle to establish peace and security in this troubled world. In that connection the minister said yesterday:
Canada has made a good and effective contribution, and her prestige stands high among the nations of the world.
To my mind that was sheer understatement. I think he might have said, had he not been too modest, that Canada has made an outstanding contribution, and that her prestige stands very high in the world today.
[Mr. Campney.l
Finally, I believe the department has indirectly made a great contribution to the growing unity of this country and the development of our nation. Our active participation in the United Nations organization I believe has brought our people closer together than ever before, has made every Canadian feel a greater pride in his country, and has stimulated the Canadian spirit to the point where the development of this country and its vast resources has begun to move forward at an unprecedented pace.
It is an historical fact that after each of the two world wars Canada, by reason of her policies, the valour of her armed forces and the energy of her participation, took a marked step forward in her influence in international affairs. I think it is equally historically true but possibly not as well known that every extension of Canadian influence in the field of world affairs has been inevitably followed by a corresponding forward step at home along the road to nationhood.
Following world war I, Canada was admitted for the first time to a peace conference in her own right. We won our own representation at the league of nations. We won the right to enter into treaties on our own behalf and to establish our own representation abroad.
These developments in the field of external affairs were paralleled at home by a whole series of constitutional developments which culminated in the Statute of Westminster, which marked the final stage of transition from a colonial empire to a commonwealth of independent nations.
Following world war II our progress in the field of world affairs is well known to all. The forward steps in this field are again being paralleled in this very parliament and at this very session by changes in our constitutional set-up. I refer to the change in the status of our supreme court and the change in the method of amending our constitution. These changes are following a pattern. We seem to make headway first in the field of international affairs and then we catch up at home.
The increasing importance of our country, owing to its outstanding participation in world affairs as we move along the road of destiny, is due in a large part to the important role played by the Department of External Affairs. In a sense, that department is becoming the mirror in which Canada is seeing herself in her true proportions for the first time. If I am right in that, the

modest estimates of the department which are the subject of the resolution before the house probably represent the most fruitful [DOT]expenditure which this house will be called upon to approve.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON STATEMENT OF MR. PEARSON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to extend any more compliments to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I am afraid that he may think he has the problems of the world settled. I believe he deserves the tributes that he has received this morning, but I should like to remind him that he has to return to Lake Success and face Vishinsky and a few other people who may not believe all the things we have heard about him in this chamber. I appreciate the difficulties facing the minister, but I believe he is a great improvement over what we previously had in external affairs.
For some time there was no Secretary of State for External Affairs and the department was pigeonholed with the Prime Minister. He had very little time to devote to the many complicated problems that are involved in international affairs. As a result of that not many discussions such as we are having at this time took place. I have listened attentively to the discussion so far. This morning we heard two addresses and, without detracting from any of the others, I believe the addresses of the member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. MacKenzie) and the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) gave us the picture from a practical standpoint.
The member for Lambton-Kent gave us a description based on his personal experience. I thought it was valuable. It is worth reading. I was rather surprised at my friend the member for Eglinton, and quite pleased. I believe he justified the existence of the parliamentary association. Because of a trip he was able to take through the medium of that association, he was able to give the house a complete, and I think fair, picture of what he saw in the different countries he visited. It was an encouraging picture. His report, and he is always inclined to be quite critical, was to the effect that progress is being made despite a lot of the press statements to the contrary. I believe the house owes something to the hon. member for the effort he made this morning. It was a fair and reasoned approach to the whole problem. The hon. member even gave credit to the government where credit was due, something that is very unusual for him. It means something, coming from him.
I should like to express my own thoughts on this particular subject. First, I should
External Affairs
like to say that since the end of the war I have thought there has been too much stress placed on war. A reading of the newspapers of the United States and Canada would lead one to believe that we are on the verge of war, and that war is inevitable. I believe that is far from the truth. Since the end of the war, my thought has been the other way. I believe that one of the greatest instruments for the maintenance of peace in the future is the United Nations organization. It is an organization that is working under great difficulties. We realize that. I have heard opinions expressed that the old league of nations failed and the United Nations is going to fail. The old league of nations did not fail. In my opinion, an ideal was sown at that time and the league struggled under great handicaps. It was hamstrung and betrayed in the work it was attempting to do in that period in which it functioned. Nevertheless the idea was sown and it is as a result of that idea that the United Nations is functioning today. It is benefiting from the experience of the old league of nations.
I said the United Nations was working under difficulties. Perhaps one of the main reasons for those difficulties is the lack of understanding between Russia and the western world. This is largely due to the propaganda that was disseminated during the war. For many years before the war the people of this country were led to believe that Russia was everything that was not right. Then Russia became our ally in the war, and immediately the propaganda machine in this continent went into reverse. It went out of its way to lead the people of North America to believe that Russia is a fine country. For some time the press was filled with stories that Russia was not irreligious, the churches were free. We all remember those statements. Even J. S. McLean of Canada Packers travelled around the country raising funds for Russia. That was only a few years ago, and today the people you are trying to convince that Russia is disturbing the peace of the world are the people this propaganda led to believe that Russia was a fine country. The man on the street is now wondering where he is going to draw the line of demarcation between propaganda and fact. That is one of the difficulties with which the United Nations has to contend at this time.
Various members have made suggestions that we are not receiving sufficient information about what is happening at Lake Success. I believe that is correct. When the minister returns to Lake Success, perhaps he

External Affairs
could see to it that everything that happens there receives full publicity in this country and the United States. Unfortunately it is impossible to get the story through to Russia. If we can keep our own people on an even keel and dispel the illusion that war is inevitable, in my opinion that will go a long way toward the maintenance of peace in this world.
There is a great deal of controversy about what the United Nations is doing and what it is not doing. In my opinion it has failed in two respects. First, it has failed to put into operation the machinery that was provided by the charter. I am not saying that is the fault of anyone because there have been difficulties in that direction. That is what made the North Atlantic pact necessary.
In discussing the charter we in this house were led to believe that an international police force was going to be set up. The military staffs of each country, under the supervision and direction of the security council, were going to get together and, on a per capita basis, were going to establish a police force that would supervise the peace of the world. I know that, as far as we are concerned and as far as the United States and the other countries within that body are concerned, that would have been done. Russia has been the stumbling block in that direction.
Then the illusion is created in the minds of a great many people across the country that the North Atlantic pact is something that has not anything to do with the league of nations, that it is an instrument that has been built by warmongers in order to make war on Soviet Russia. That opinion is current in some sectors of our society. But that is not true either. The North Atlantic pact was made absolutely necessary because of the failure of the United Nations, because of Russia's opposition to forming the international police force which is to provide the machinery if and when it is set up. The Atlantic pact is an outgrowth of the United Nations. The charter makes provision for the setting up of regional pacts if that is necessary. Hence the Atlantic pact is set up, and I am glad that it is; because in linking up the nations that form that pact for economic and military purposes, it is a step in the right direction. But in my opinion that machinery should go a little bit further.
While there is a certain amount of economic arrangement within the North Atlantic pact, in the United States and Canada I think there is a growing opinion that not only should it be a military and a partial economic pact but that we should go further with that machinery and that there should be an alliance of the nations that are set up today,
[Mr. Gffiis.l
a union of these countries, for all purposes. Following that idea to its logical conclusion, I think that eventually within that structure we should perhaps have a common currency, and trade arrangements which would eliminate many of the difficulties we are having today. That opinion is becoming strong in the United States and in many sections of Canada where people are thinking and reading; because the future of the world on the road ahead is, in my opinion, within the structure of those united nations in following through these ideas.
Another place where I think we have fallen down is in implementing the machinery set up at Bretton Woods for the purpose of stabilizing currency and developing backward countries. These principles were enunciated in the Atlantic charter. They were discussed in this house and all over the country. To Bretton Woods were sent the ablest men in finance in Canada, the United States and in every other country. My friends in the Social Credit party say that the Bretton Woods agreement failed. But it did not fail. It was not tried.

speechtext:
The international bank and the international monetary fund were outgrowths of the Bretton Woods agreement. The fund was established. The forty-five nations that are now members of the United Nations are members of that international bank and international monetary fund. Some $750 million was subscribed, but that bank has never functioned. If it had functioned for the purpose for which it was intended, we would not have had devaluation of Britain's currency. We would not have the mess there is in certain parts of the world today if we had accepted our responsibilities, through the medium of that financial machinery, to develop backward countries and to give them a chance to get on their feet. The Marshall plan has, to some extent, done that; but it has not been a united effort on the part of the forty-five nations that are members of that international bank and international monetary fund. As for myself, I think that particular subject has been overlooked; at least, I cannot find that it has been discussed at all in the United Nations.
I am merely making these observations to direct the minister's thoughts to these points so that when he goes back, in addition to attending to his many other duties, he can try to do a little bit of thinking about them and to interest in them someone who happens to be on the committees that have to do with subjects of that kind. But definitely I think

we must get our own people in the United States and Canada down to more basic thinking.
Then as to this business about China: I have heard it discussed here and I had heard it discussed before I came here. Many people say that there is a move on foot now for Britain to recognize China and to do business with her. My suggestion is this. What else can she do under the circumstances? She has possessions at Hong Kong. She is standing there facing an army that conquered China. Is she going to precipitate a war on that country? I should like to leave this thought with some of the members of the house and with some outside it. China today, in my opinion, is not being invaded from the outside. She is taking the only course that is left open to her. If we stop and think for a moment, we realize that, for six or seven years before the last war broke out, China was standing practically alone fighting the invasion of fascism from Japan-bombed, starved, and all the rest of it. Then in 1941, when she was in desperate straits, somebody closed the Burma road on her and thereby closed off the only route through which she could take in supplies and carry on resistance. After war was declared by Germany, Japan was supplied with scrap from this country. China has been in a terrible mess; and the people of China today are taking the only means by which they can provide themselves with some security, a means of livelihood and a means of developing their own country.
I see them taking that position because there is no other road out for them. Chiang Kai-shek is trying to maintain the status quo. While I have heard some hon. members defending his regime, yet there are some pretty black pages in that regime when it comes to ruthlessness and all that goes with it. Let us not get the idea that China must be isolated. In my opinion she took the only way out of her present difficulties that she could. We have to come to an understanding with her.
With regard to Russia, let us not forget that it was dictatorship, tyranny and everything that goes with it that compelled these people to seek the only way out. I have no quarrel with them for what they are doing in their own country, because they never had freedom, they never had democracy. Eighty-five per cent of them are illiterate, and they have practically no standard of living. They took the only way out in their own country. Where I quarrel with them is in what they are trying to do outside their own country. I have nothing but contempt, and have had nothing but contempt for the last twenty-five years,
External Affairs
for anyone who calls himself a Canadian or an American and becomes an ally of that particular kind of organization within Canada But let us not forget that it was hunger, poverty, the absence of security, and misery that drove these people in the direction in which they are going at the present time. There was no alternative for them; but there is on this continent. We have to demonstrate to the people of the outside world that we are prepared to see their problems as they really are and do what we can to help them restore freedom in their countries.
There has to be a lot of basic thinking and a lot of careful talking on these particular subjects. I am not unmindful of the fact- and of course most of the hon. members are not-that while today, on this continent, we have the highest standard of living in the world, and our mass production is unequalled, yet we must not forget that it is not many years ago that Britain was in that position. Our resources are not inexhaustible. In the not too distant future, in terms of generations, we may find another continent giving world leadership. India and China have vast sources of wealth. These countries, with their millions and millions of people who are just beginning to tap their resources, may become world leaders. We have to understand one another and try to work together. In my opinion the United Nations is providing that leadership. We are fortunate in having the man there that we have. I believe that our present Secretary of State for External Affairs, with his background, his knowledge of international affairs over the years, is contributing in a valuable way to that end. I hope that he does not develop the complex that we are a little country and that we should not have too much to say; because one man who is honest and knows where he is going in that organization, whether he represent a little country or a big one, may be able to sell to the big countries ideas that will stick in the future. I think we have in that organization a man of whom we can be proud. I hope he does not get a swelled head and develop a statesmanship complex. I like to think of him as just plain honest Mike. I hope he remains that way.
The difficulties that are being created are exemplified in a little editorial which I picked out of the last issue of the Western Co-Operator. I am not going to read it. In this editorial it is stated that a man in the United States by the name of Armstrong had $50 million which he wanted to give to a certain university with the stipulation that no negroes or Asiatics were to be admitted. He was to write the bylaws of the university. The university was to do what he asked. That is the old Hitler complex. It is quite difficult

External Affairs
for a man to sit on the United Nations organization under present world conditions when that kind of stuff is sent abroad. Here is a man who is a big industrialist. He is very influential in the affairs of the United States, and he comes up with a proposal of that kind. I can hear radio Moscow picking it up and saying: "Here are the people who are looking for co-operation. This is the kind of thing that they are doing behind the scenes at a time when they are making a lot of promises within the United Nations organization."

I do not want to delay this debate any longer. I merely wanted to express my opinion along these lines. Through the United Nations we should try to do a job with the international monetary fund. We should try to make it function. I believe there is a solution there for the difficulties of world currencies. If that bank were working properly it could do a good job there. It is staffed well. It has made a good start, but it is not functioning as it should. If it were it would go a long way toward helping the people in the backward countries. These were the principles upon which we fought the war and it is upon these principles that we established the structure of the North Atlantic pact. It is an idea that is workable. It is what made the United States. It is the same pattern. There is no reason why we cannot do it on an international scale. There is a large body of public opinion in the United States and Canada in favour of it now. We should go forward with it carefully and see that it works properly.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of Ihe Opposition):

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON STATEMENT OF MR. PEARSON
speechtext:
One thing that has been very noticeable in this debate has been the obvious spirit of agreement that within this chamber there should be no difference of purpose in regard to the objectives of this country in relation to the very simple but very ominous threat that faces us and faces the rest of the world. Probably at no time has the responsibility imposed upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs, or the corresponding members of government in other countries, been heavier than it is at the present time. It would appear that never before have the issues been so clearly in focus as they have been during this past year, and they seem to be becoming more clearly in focus all the time.
Everything that has been said since the Secretary of State for External Affairs gave

his very comprehensive review of the position of his department and the basis upon which the Canadian government is approaching these great problems today has been an attempt to contribute something to a greater appreciation of various aspects of this problem. And everything that has been said has been more with the hope of adding something to a general appreciation of this great problem than to be critical of any point of view that has been expressed, or to minimize in any way the significance of the summary that was made in this house yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It is from that point of view that I should like to emphasize some features of the present situation which I believe all of us should bear in mind in expressing our opinions now and in seeking to play our part in awakening a lively public interest in the subject that we are discussing, and in creating the opinion in the minds of the people of Canada that this is the business of every Canadian; and that the whole future of Canada, as well as the future of free people elsewhere throughout the world, will depend upon the extent to which people themselves, who still have the greatest concern about what happens, devote their thoughts to this subject and express their opinions as to how they think world events should be faced by the government of this country in the years ahead.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has outlined the situation with which the countries are confronted in view of the attitude of the representatives of Russia at this time. I should like to underline the words "representatives of Russia at this time". I do not believe that the people of Russia themselves are reluctant in any way to establish a basis of friendship with the other nations of the world if that opportunity were only open to them.
Unfortunately under the system of rigid dictatorship which has been imposed upon the 200 million people of Russia itself, and upon more than 500 million others throughout the world in these past four years, there is little opportunity for the people to know what other people are thinking. Unfortunately the people of Russia, and those others living under communist dictatorship elsewhere, are unaware of the fact that throughout the free world the people in that free world want nothing more than an opportunity to demonstrate their real friendship for the people of Russia, and of every other country in the world.
Unhappily it would not serve the purposes of the communistic dictatorship to let their people know that this spirit of friendship does exist; and consequently not only is a

barrier being created between them and the free world, which prevents access to their country by the people of the free world, but equally they are preventing people living behind the iron curtain from knowing anything about the way the rest of the world really lives, and what the sentiments of the rest of the world really are.
There is one feature of the present situation which it does seem to me is too reminiscent of what happened in the years before the last war. It is a feature which perhaps is not discussed often enough in approaching the problem we face today. When the nations which had been joined in arms to destroy the military power of Germany and Germany's associates in that war met at San Francisco before the war had actually ended to draft a charter which would provide a working basis for co-operation between those nations which had been associated in that terrible conflict on the side of freedom, the very beginning of that charter was the proposition that every nation had the right to choose its own form of government, and that no nation in the world would have a form of government imposed upon it by any outside power.
That was the foundation upon which the whole concept of the charter of the United Nations was drafted. It applied to Russia just as it applied to China and as it applied to every other country which signed that charter. It was also intended ultimately to apply to those countries which were then ranged as enemies against the nations whose representatives met at San Francisco in 1945.
As we discuss the external affairs of this country today, and our association with the nations of the Atlantic community in an effort to preserve their freedom within the circumstances which now confront us, it is essential that we remember how far that basic proposition has already been denied. We are not simply in a position where we are preventing Russia from denying it. Russia has already denied it; she has repudiated that proposition and has carried aggression to a point far beyond what Germany had done up to the outbreak of war in September of 1939. And we shall not be facing reality unless we keep that truth in mind.
Russia is not only today threatening the freedom of the western world both by its accumulation of military power and by its fifth column organized in every free country, but also has already imposed its will by force upon one nation after another which had no more desire to submit to communist dictatorship than we have here in Canada
External Affairs
today. The Baltic states of Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia are countries with a tradition of freedom, countries which have demonstrated a love of freedom which makes communist dictatorship no more acceptable to them than it would be to us.
Poland throughout long years had cherished a love of freedom and had asserted that love in the struggle it had made against Germany in 1939. It would always be well for us to remember that in September of that year we did not go to war as a free people by our own choice because our soil was attacked. We went to war because Poland at that time had become the symbol of the right of every nation to have its own form of government and to have its own territorial integrity respected. This country went to war when Poland was attacked because we, along with other free countries, recognized at that time that if aggression of that kind was permitted to carry forward its terrible course, it would only be a question of time before the right of any nation anywhere to have its own form of government would be destroyed. And as we see Poland today, under the iron heel of communism, at this very hour undergoing one of those purges directed from Moscow, which means that any pretence of legal authority is hypocrisy of the worst kind, we might well bear in mind that it was the attack on Poland in 1939 that brought the United Kingdom, France, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, India and the other parts of the great British fellowship into this conflict.
Then, as we look at the other countries throughout Europe which have been placed under communist domination, whether they had democracy or not before that form of government was set up, at least they had their own form of government. And under the United Nations charter-the very first chapter of it-they had a right to have their freedom respected and to have their own form of government chosen by themselves.
One by one we have seen Roumania, Hungary, Bulgaria, Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia, along with other smaller nations, brought under communist control and dictatorship from the Kremlin. It is not likely that more than ten per cent of the people of Czechoslovakia at the very outside supported even to a limited extent the ideas of communism prior to the time that the dictatorship was set up there early last year. That is a warning as to what can happen elsewhere, and as it happened in Czechoslovakia it is well for us to remember that when communism came to Russia in 1917 less than two per cent of the people subscribed to communist doctrines or were

External Affairs
members of the communist party. A small compact minority with military power has demonstrated what it can do in any land.
During the last year the greatest tragedy since the war has taken place and China has been brought under communist domination. In the review of the situation which was given to us yesterday, it was indicated that there would be certain requirements which must be fulfilled before the communist government of China could be recognized. As I understand, one of them was that there should be evidence that this was a government that was accepted by the people of China. We have no way of testing the acceptance of a communist government in any land because once a communist government is set up acceptance of it is not a matter of free choice but is enforced upon the people by rifles and machine guns, and every device of suppression known to man. Therefore, if that is to be the test, I submit there can be no recognition of the communist government of China.
The pattern is clear. The government there will, as in every other land, still be a government subservient to the Kremlin, and if in any country the people should seek to assert their national beliefs as something separate from international communism undoubtedly it will be greeted in the same way as the assertion of that right was greeted when the communist government of Yugoslavia expressed the simple belief that they were first of all Yugoslavs, and that they did not believe the communist doctrine meant they must of necessity submit to controls from the Kremlin. These events are moving so fast that not one of us can see clearly yet what may happen in Yugoslavia. Any one of a number of events may occur. In any case, it is unlikely that things will just stand still.
Although we detest communism as a doctrine, I imagine that every Canadian will welcome the assertion of Yugoslav pride in their own national integrity, and will hope that the people of Yugoslavia, under whatever form of government they have, will be able to retain control over their own affairs free from domination by the Kremlin. If they succeed in doing that, then it may well be a hopeful and encouraging sign to those other lands now under communist governments that they too can do the same thing. Step by step, if nations are able to free themselves from the domination and control of the Russian communist party, as distinguished from the communist parties in their own lands, the day will be that much nearer when there may be some hope that the people of

these countries will evolve a free system of government which will in fact become a democracy as we understand it.
Prepared as the nations of the Atlantic community are today to do what is necessary to preserve our freedom, it is essential that we all remember that we shall not have carried out our full purpose merely by the preservation of our own freedom. If we believe in the charter of the United Nations, this will only be the first vital step. Nothing can be more vital to any one of us than the preservation of our free system of government, but when we have assured the preservation of that freedom in our own country we still must remember that, to the extent that we still assert our belief in the principles of the United Nations charter, we must do what we can in the days ahead to assure the acceptance of the doctrine that every nation has a right to determine its own course. We must do what we can to bring to those nations which have been brought under Russian domination the hope of freedom that was extended to them when the nations signed that great charter at San Francisco in 1945. Anything less than that is a denial of the very principles for which this country and the other free nations were fighting so short a time ago.
This does not mean that we must contemplate the possibility of aggressive acts of any kind. If the free nations of the west establish a position of such strength and certainty of purpose that Russia is in no doubt whatever about their determination to stand together to preserve their freedom, then we shall have gone a long way towards the fulfilment of that ideal of the United Nations charter. Russia and the nations now satellite to Russian power cannot contemplate with any degree of satisfaction a rigid division between that part of the world under communist governments and that part under free and democratic governments on the other side of the iron curtain. There are many	things	that	Russia	needs	for	thedevelopment of her vast territory. There are many	things	that	Russia	needs	for	the
restoration of her damaged cities and countryside which can only be obtained from the free countries of the west. There are many skills and techniques that Russia needs to assist them in their hope of development in the years ahead.
If the free nations of the west, the nations of the Atlantic community, stand firm and leave no doubt about their purpose, the time may well come-and sooner than many of us may hope today-when it will be possible to say to Russia: Carry out the provisions of the Atlantic charter. Free

Poland; free Yugoslavia; free Bulgaria and Roumania; free the Baltic states; free Czechoslovakia and China from your threat of power. Leave them free to make their own choice, in their own way. Then we shall be prepared to say we do not pretend to tell you what form of government you should have within your own land; and if you give that evidence of acceptance of the charter we shall recognize you as a member of the great fellowship which was established at San Francisco.
That is not an impossible dream or hope. In fact it is the only hope of sanity in the years ahead. It is the only hope for a steady growth of freedom in those lands which have known freedom but which today are under communist control. But the starting point is the firmness of purpose and effective co-operation of the nations now associated in that famous pact, who have been brought together for the preservation of their own freedom and for no other purpose, certainly none which could threaten any other nation.
Here in Canada, as elsewhere, it becomes increasingly important that our intentions be clear beyond doubt. For that reason I want to point out a kind of uncertainty which it seems to me should be removed here in our own country, for it is the kind of uncertainty which may cause confusion in the minds of our people and of people outside Canada. In a speech in this house on November 11 the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) said, as reported at page 1698 of Hansard:
It is perfectly clear that we have no commitments whatever under the North Atlantic treaty.
He went on to indicate that as a result of subsequent discussions which might take place certain commitments might be considered by the government. But I would like to compare his words with those of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) yesterday, as they appear at page 1843 of Hansard:
In broad terms, we are committed to provide such aid as we can reasonably be expected to contribute, in the form in which we can most effectively furnish it.
I think no doubt should be left in the mind of any member of this house, and no doubt should be left in the minds of the people of Canada, as to our actual position. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, who is the member of the government responsible for our external policies and their expression, has said that in broad terms we are committed to provide such aid as we can reasonably be expected to contribute, in the form in which we can most effectively furnish it; while the Minister of National Defence, who would be 45781-120
External Affairs
responsible for the form any military preparation would take, has stated that we have no commitments. This may be simply a difference in the use of the same terms, but I do believe any doubt created by those two expressions should be removed so that no one in this house and no Canadian would be in any uncertainty as to what actually is our position.
This is more than the matter of the definition of a sentence or the particular use of a word. It was out of uncertainties that the last war crept upon us and ultimately became almost unavoidable. We have heard a great deal of what happened in China, and none of us can be for a moment unaware of the direct effect those tragic events have upon this country as a Pacific nation. We should remember that the first dangerous weakening of the league of nations and the first dangerous departure from the principles set out in the covenant occurred when Japan was permitted to carry forward its aggression in Manchuria in 1931 and the years following, with no effective steps taken by those nations which could have asserted their voice and prevented that aggression without a shot being fired.
Hon. members will recall that a commission of great leaders of thought from Canada, Great Britain, the United States, France and other nations went to China and reported upon the situation there. The Canadian leading that delegation was the late Mr. Justice Rowell. Hon members will also recall that it was pointed out that the failure of the nations, who had joined in the league of nations to preserve peace, to act at that time marked the beginning of a steady weakening of that association which had been formed after the first world war to prevent a repetition of that tragedy. Then came the Italian occupation of Ethiopia; then came the German invasion of the Rhineland.
Step by step aggression moved forward, and no effective voices were raised in unity of purpose or in clarity of expression which said to the aggressor nations, "We meant what we said when we signed the charter of the league of nations at Versailles in 1919." Many times since the end of the last war numbers of people have been subjected to acts of aggression. Although the nations of the Atlantic community are joining to preserve their own freedom today, no united voice has been raised to challenge that aggression which has been taking place in the rest of the world in a manner which would stem that flood. For that reason it is essential that we in Canada have no doubt where we stand, and that the

External Affairs
nations with whom we are associated have no doubt where we stand. We should have no doubt where they stand.
In 1939 the people who lived in the free nations said that never again would the word appeasement be written in letters of blood across the face of the world. There has been appeasement. Perhaps that appeasement was unavoidable, but there has been appeasement. Now the nations of the Atlantic community are taking a stand in the face of the threat which confronts them. The effectiveness of the new pact for the preservation of our freedom will depend upon the extent to which each of the member nations knows exactly what that pact means. Whatever it means, let us be quite clear about it. It is only to the extent that we are clear that the nations who are associated together can hope to carry forward the great purposes they have undertaken.
Whatever limitations there are, let those limitations be disclosed. Whatever commitments there are, let those commitments be stated with clarity and without reserve. Whatever the basis of co-operation is, let us, as the elected representatives of the people, know what that basis is so that, through the reporting of the proceedings here, the people of Canada will know exactly what our part is going to be. Let us not once again be uncertain as to what it is we are undertaking or what the course is upon which we have actually embarked. For that reason I would hope that the remarks of the minister which will sum up this debate will clarify those points.
Yesterday, in his comprehensive and constructive speech following that of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) referred to the importance of the use of atomic energy for industrial purposes. He referred to statements that have been made about the difficulty of developing industrial uses while we are still under the threat of the military use of the atom bomb. To the extent that it may be certain that Russia actually has the secret of the atom bomb in practical form, then it would seem that the necessity for some measure of secrecy may have been removed-at any rate in regard to certain processes related to the use of nuclear energy. To the extent that Russia already has knowledge of this great development with its many possibilities for peace, it would seem that the development of this source of energy for peaceful purposes could be extended without fear of any disclosure to a nation that could use that knowledge against us at some time in the future if we were not able to find a peaceful solution to our differences.

As has been pointed out, it may well be that this discovery will usher in the greatest advancement in human welfare in the history of the world. If that immense power can be directed to peaceful ends, then the opportunity for human advancement and for the reduction of human energy in certain activities will have been carried forward to a great degree. Canada is in a unique position to open up opportunities associated with this great discovery. As has been suggested, we need not approach the problems associated with this dramatic discovery with any feeling of limitation because we are a nation of less than 14 million in a world of so many hundreds of millions. The very fact that we are still a nation with a relatively small population opens special opportunities for us to speak with a voice which cannot be suspected because of the certainty that under no conceivable circumstances could we have, any aggressive designs.
I believe it can be said, to the credit of those who have spoken on behalf of Canada at the United Nations' meetings and elsewhere, that the Canadian voice has been heard and that all of us welcome the extent to which Canada's opinion is respected in the councils of the nations of the world.
As we go into the years immediately ahead, years which perhaps will be more fateful than any that we have ever known, those who speak on behalf of Canada will undoubtedly receive the wholehearted support of every member of this house and of every Canadian to the extent that, with clarity, with courage and with constructive thought, they lay before the meetings of the nations plans which will be the basis for possible peace in the years ahead.
We can play a great part because of our unique position as the immediate neighbour of the most powerful single nation of the world and as a partner in that great free fellowship which has been evolving throughout the centuries and which is now a partnership of free nations within the British commonwealth. On the one hand, we are partners with a group of nations with a similar system of government and with a common loyalty to fundamental principles of freedom; and we are the immediate and friendly associate of that other great nation which today is playing such a major role in the preservation of peace. We are in a unique position to be the interpreter to the British fellowship of the point of view of those living on the North American continent; and we are in an equally unique position to interpret to those living on this continent the point of view of those who are associated in that wider world

fellowship. It is a great challenge to every one of us. It is a challenge which places almost no limit upon the opportunity that exists for the representatives of this country to make an effective contribution to the possibility of peace and world-wide understanding in the years ahead.
I have sought to emphasize the point that the great lesson of the years between the two world wars is as to clarity of purpose and the extent to which the nations leave no doubt about their purpose if peace is to be preserved. The nations which met in San Francisco drafted this new pact which they hoped would avoid the weaknesses which had destroyed the hopes of those who joined in the league of nations. The nations which met at San Francisco were determined that never again would the horrible tragedy of those years be repeated if it was within the power of nations working in co-operation to prevent it. It is for that reason that, within such a limited area as the Atlantic pact can operate and ultimately in that wider area embraced by the United Nations charter, each of us should keep alive today the lessons of those tragic years that made the second world war possible-a war which definitely could have been avoided, by all the evidence that is before us today, if the free nations of the world had stood together at that time as they are standing together now.
It is vital that the people of this country and of the other countries be brought fully into the confidence of their governments. It is vital to the success of any plans that are made that the people of each of those countries be brought into wholehearted support of them. For that reason this house not only welcomes the discussion which has taken place on this occasion but will certainly welcome at all times in the future the explanations that can be given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) or by any other member of the government of the plans that are under way for the preservation of peace and the strengthening of international harmony and good will. This is one subject on which none of us can be divided in purpose, no matter whether in detail any of us may hold a different opinion. The statements that have been made here, and the views that have been expressed from every part of this house, have, I know, been made only in the hope that they may strengthen the hand of the minister and the hand of the government in playing our part as a nation at this important time in our history, so that we may take our part in preserving that peace for which so many of the finest of our youth gave their lives so short a time ago.

speechtext:
1
was delighted, Mr. Speaker, to listen to the fine oratorical effort of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). It shows that he can do well any time that he leaves politics aside.

Last evening I heard the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) say that prayers should be said for peace. How many people tell their children never to forget when saying their prayers at night, when their

arms are on their little beds, to pray that at last peace may reign on earth? Christmas is coming; peace has been promised to men of good will. So I hope that the prayers of children as well as the prayers of men will be well understood by God, and that finally we shall have that peace for which everyone is praying.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I saw, a few moments ago, ominous clouds gather on our small community, the House of Commons, I felt I should speak in French, in a language I would like to make as beautiful and as clear as when Corneille, Racine and others spoke it, so that it may act as a ray of resplendent sunshine. But need I really compare this beautiful language to a ray of sunshine, since the words of peace and understanding spoken by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), when he concluded his speech, have dispelled those clouds as if by magic and have given us a striking example of what international co-operation and peace may accomplish.
Mr. Speaker, like all other members, I usually pay a great deal of attention to requests submitted to me by my constituents. Since we are dealing with external affairs, I feel I should put on record a request submitted to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) by the Sacred Heart leagues in my constituency and elsewhere, especially by the league from Donnacona, for the internationalization of the Holy Land.
I shall not quote the whole resolution; I can, however, tell the house that public opinion in my constituency is strongly in favour of the project. On the other hand, I am quite sure that the government will draw the attention of the United Nations to this matter which is of such particular interest at the moment.
I wish to join the previous speakers in congratulating the Secretary of State foi External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). I know it is unnecessary, but I do so just the same. Our representative at the United Nations acquits himself so well of his duties that any hon. member who speaks during this most important debate cannot help but compliment the minister, who so fully deserves it. I also wish to pay tribute to the other delegates who accompanied him to Lake Success, and in doing so I am sure that I express the feelings of the house.
At one time, whenever I intended taking part in a debate, my friends used to ask me, "Will you speak of communism?"

When the house adjourned this morning, a friend of mine, who is one of the youngest and most brilliant members of the house, asked me whether I would discuss Spain in this debate. In order to follow the traditional practice and to preserve the good fellowship which should prevail among members of the house, I have decided to ask those who share my opinion to urge the United Nations organization to give kinder and greater consideration to the various requests concerning Spain's admission to the organization, as a party to the Atlantic pact.
Mr. Salazar, who is recognized as the most liberal dictator in existence, recently appealed for the admission of Spain to the United Nations organization. I do not know whether his words will carry enough weight to convince the leaders of the organization.
Here, I wish to refer to something the hon. member for Temiscouata said a while ago when he spoke about the great powers' veto. I would ask the supporters of this right of veto-and I am not now criticizing or censuring anyone in this house-whether or not they feel the right of veto granted to the Big Three is dictatorial in nature, since they are using it to bar Spain from membership in the United Nations, under the pretext that it is now led by dictator Franco.
Can we not think that the word "logic" has lost its meaning? If dictatorial behaviour is countenanced within the United Nations organization why not admit the thought of including a liberal dictator like Franco-or Mr. Salazar?
I fail to see why, within the United Nations or elsewhere, there should be any objection to Spain's admission. Is it simply because Franco is being held in derision and pointed at, because he is a dictator?
Present democracies and the greater part of those who are members of the United Nations certainly have had friendly relations with dictators of the past. A king has been known to seek help from a dictator, to restore order in his country. So it was that, in 1923, King Alfonso XIII called upon Primo de Rivera to become a military dictator and to lead a full-fledged dictatorship.
If you will refer to the Encyclopaedia Britannica you will read about the circumstances surrounding Primo de Rivera's advent as head of the Spanish army, where he was called by a king. How ironical that those very nations which did not protest against Primo 45781-121
External Affairs
de Rivera's leadership should now deny Spain the right and privilege to sit beside other nations of the world in the councils of the United Nations.
Besides, Canada itself, if it did not directly help Franco into power, at least made things somewhat easier for him. In 1937 this very house passed a law which, in effect, prevented Canadian nationals from enlisting in the Spanish republic army to fight Franco. It is chapter 32 of the Statutes of Canada. It may therefore be said that we facilitated Franco's ascent to power. That is why I cannot understand that we should now deny Spain, and Franco, the right to belong to the United Nations organization.
Mr. Speaker, there are other dictators. Our friend Salazar, a dictator, is and always has been a friend of England, especially during the war. Fulgentio Batista of Cuba was a dictator but never incurred the displeasure of the United States. When England and the United States are considering ways and means to make peace with Yugoslavia, and to grant her a loan, does it not seem like a gesture that is-I will not say ridiculous, because it would be too harsh a word-but illogical?
At the present time Tito, even though he is dictator of Yugoslavia and seems to be drawing away from Stalin, nevertheless remains an avowed and earnest communist. Recently he was up to his tricks with England and at a meeting of the executive of the Yugoslav communist party, even went so far as to say:
The atomic bomb is a new factor with which the forces of capitalism want to destroy the Soviet union and the victorious hopes of the working class. It is their only hope . . .
We did not quite reach our goal because ever since 1945 production of the atomic bomb was accelerated and improved upon. However, we are not far short of our aims. We need a little more time, however, to reorganize our troops and complete our preparations with arms and munitions. For the time being we will therefore follow a middle-of-the-road policy so as to gain time and to achieve industrial reconstruction within the Soviet union and other countries under its control.
I hate to think that he would use American and British loans to achieve industrial reconstruction within the Soviet union and other countries under its control. Tito continues:
Then the time will come to launch into the battle for the final extermination of reaction.
Our first target is Great Britain, even though public opinion ranks it second in importance and considers our forces should rally instead against the United States. We must never forget that Great Britain is very influential on four continents.
There is a man who today receives loans from two great countries which, moreover, officially recognize his government. These

External Affairs
two great countries, however, refuse to acknowledge Spain among the nations, as she is entitled to be. It is not because he is a Roman Catholic and that I am too that I speak on behalf of Franco, but from a strategic point of view. I believe Spain could exert a beneficial influence among the nations of the North Atlantic pact. If Spain were afforded a more serious, more adequate, more real and more rational consideration, the world would largely benefit therefrom, because, as I said before in the house, quoting Goethe:
Spain is at the gateway of the Mediterranean sea. The nation holding Constantinople will hold power over the world.
Constantinople is at the gateway of the Mediterranean sea. Mr. Speaker, let us suppose for a moment-although I shall never believe it might come to pass-that the whole of Europe becomes the prey of communism- I do not say of Russia, but of communism. Let us suppose that Spain should remain the only fortress and in my opinion she is now the strongest fortress against communism in Europe and in the world, next to Canada.
Supposing that the remainder of Europe, both coasts of the Mediterranean, for instance, should be occupied by forces under the control of Russia, what would happen, strategically and economically, to the remnant of the great British empire? What will happen if the United States and Canada have to face alone a nation stronger in armaments and manpower, and contend against its ideology? We should not disregard the ever-increasing [DOT] force of Russia and her ideology.
Because the nations are unwilling to place their discussions upon a reasonable and logical basis, that is the respect of the human being, their negotiations will not bring the desired results and the co-operation which would be necessary for the establishment of world peace will be lacking. It is imperative that the nations should be alive to the situation. As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said a few minutes ago, they have the right to choose whatever government they want.
In saying this, I do not neglect Spain which has a government to its liking. Some people declaim very strongly against the Spanish government. Yet, in this world of ours, peoples like individuals have a character of their own; but too often, unfortunately, international associations do not recognize this fact.
Knowing the character of the Spaniards and the human geography of Spain, one has

to conclude that that country now has the kind of government which will enable it to regain the economic stability which was denied its people, even by the republic of 1931.
Some people give as their idle pretext for refusing to admit Spain within the United Nations that Franco's government has persecuted and is still persecuting various religious denominations. They are completely wrong. Those that have been persecuted by Franco's government were guilty of political activity as politicians. They were not persecuted because of their religious beliefs, but because they wanted to overthrow Franco, in order to replace his regime by their own clique. Then the Spaniards, who want to live like other people, would first be under a so-called republican rule, and later under communist domination.
I have in my hand an article by a man quite familiar with Spanish affairs, Mr. Richard Pattee, in which he states that those who know the Spanish temperament are aware that at the present time only Franco's dictatorship can keep Spaniards united. I realize that the word "dictatorship" has an unpleasant ring in many ears. Yet those who wince at the sound of it would be prepared to set up another dictatorship, even more rigid, such as that which now exists in Russia, a state dictatorship.
At first, this type of dictatorship is content to nationalize this or that industry. It then goes on to nationalize medicine and, in so doing utterly destroys the true character of the doctor. It then nationalizes steel mills and transports, and so the dictatorship keeps on and grows apace.
Recently, two English bishops or archbishops offered advice to the labour-socialist government of Great Britain. What happened? Two members of the British cabinet, Messrs. Shinwell and Cripps, felt called upon to issue a tart warning to England's church authorities not to meddle with affairs of the nation. Once again and strangely enough that was glaringly illogical. Government spokesmen requested the guardians of the nation's morals not to meddle with politics. Now the very politicians who chided them for defending morals now admit that England is going through a moral crisis, thus justifying the men who sought to help the government.
Mr. Speaker, a fairly long time ago there lived in Europe a man remarkable for his tenacity, his courage and his methodical work. I am not praising him, I am just stating facts

and describing this man who had such a pleasant disposition that he was called "Dr. Cranky". That man was Karl Marx, who knew the country's history well enough.
Speaking about Russia, Karl Marx stated:
Impeding the annexation policy of Russia is an all-important matter. This matter concerns all democracies and especially Great Britain and all the nations of the world must unite to prevent this invasion by Russia.
Karl Marx knew history and was aware that before the advent of communism in Russia, there was a man, Peter the Great, whom communists consider today as the forerunner of communism. Peter the Great said:
Let us deal with the east, let us look towards the east. The west is a matter of time.
Karl Marx did not know however,-because he died seventeen years too soon,-that another communist would say almost the same thing. That man was Lenin, who was born in 1870. Moreover, students of world history have realized that the annexation policy of the Czars has been overshadowed by the annexation program of the communists. Therefore those who consider Peter the Great as one of the forerunners of communism are not altogether wrong. Moreover, we have the testimonials of those who strongly believe in Peter the Great and who themselves consider him foremost among the forerunners of communism.
I heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs speak yesterday of the Middle East and the Far East. As far as that part of Asia is concerned, I still believe that the aim of Russia as well as of the communists has always been to conquer the east, and once well established in the east, to deal more successfully with the west.
I am asking and I shall keep on asking that the nations recognize Spain's desire to membership in the United Nations, not as a futile right but as an almost sacred right, a right that all the nations of the world will want to recognize if they really fear communism and the dangers which this doctrine holds for world peace. Nowadays it is really no longer a question of communist doctrine since the encroachments of Lenin, Stalin and others. In 1820, there was a movement which spread again in 1823. It was the panslavonic movement, which grew around the year 1850. Mr. Speaker, when I say panslavonic I do not mean communist, because communism diverted the real purpose of the pan-slavonic movement.
I repeat that so long as the world does not come back to the basic idea of recognizing 45781-121J
External Affairs
the sacredness of human beings and human rights, so long as those rights are not fully recognized, any declaration of human rights and privileges made at the United Nations or elsewhere will be devoid of meaning.
In concluding, I wish to say that my remarks imply no criticism, but that they are merely the expression of my own views. I never hesitate to voice my opinion. I know that other members wish to speak this afternoon, and I shall therefore let them take the floor. Before doing so, however, I wish to quote something that was said by Goethe, the old German who has achieved an outstanding place in history. I quote:
There comes a point where national hatred disappears completely, and where rising as it were above national considerations, men feel the good or ill fortune of a neighbouring people as if it were their own.
Goethe's saying should be pondered by the representatives of the United Nations who are responsible for the re-establishment of world peace. I ask that Spain be admitted to the United Nations because I think her co-operation is necessary in our continued fight against communist Russia's encroachments throughout the world and especially in Europe.
I cannot understand how two nations like the United States and Great Britain can believe that a communist like Tito could, after obtaining a loan from them, turn against communism. We ought to be certain. When a nation is ready to co-operate with the United Nations, account must be taken of the character of its people since the aim is to give her our help, our co-operation and the assurance of a better future, whereby she may continue her march toward progress. That is my wish for Spain.
