speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has been listening very patiently now for almost two whole days to excellent speeches on external affairs. I have no intention of making a speech in the ordinary sense, but I am concerned about two particular questions which I propose to place before him in the hope that when he is summing up at the end of the debate he will say something about them. The first is this. I would ask him to go further than he did yesterday in explaining Canada's policy in the Pacific. For example, there

External Affairs
appeared in the press of Tuesday and also of yesterday dispatches from London to the effect that there is to be a conference in Colombo, Ceylon, in the month of January, which will deal with the questions of recognition of the Chinese communist government and of a peace treaty with Japan. One of the dispatches does not indicate whether or not Canada will be attending, but I think the dispatch of yesterday said that it was expected that Canada would be participating in this conference. From now on I hope that the Canadian government will see to it that Canada takes a leading part in Pacific affairs.
I realize that the majority of the people of Canada live on the Atlantic slope. They face Europe. Most of the Canadians who live on the Pacific slope came either from eastern Canada or from Europe, or their parents came from eastern Canada or Europe, so that even on the Pacific slope there is almost as much interest taken in what goes on in Europe as in what goes on across the Pacific. It is readily understood why Canadians follow primarily the events across the Atlantic. But in recent years there have been drastic changes in the Pacific, and Canada is vitally affected by everything that happens around that ocean. I believe that the situation there is a good deal more serious today than it is in Europe. The Secretary of State for External Affairs used words to that effect yesterday, which may be found at page 1837 of Hansard. After dealing with the situation in Europe he said:
We have made some progress In dealing with these problems. Meanwhile, on the other side of our country scant progress has been made in coping with the great post-war problems of the Pacific area.
I believe that the policy of the United States has been a mistaken one in that that nation has not paid sufficient attention to the Pacific. I hold in my hand a pamphlet of the Behind-the-Headlines series, entitled "American Policy Abroad" by Blair Bolles, the director of the Washington bureau of the American foreign policy association. He calls the American foreign policy a "half-world policy". He says:
The weakness of American foreign policy has been its concentration on Europe. By this concentration, it has left itself exposed to developments in Asia, where the Soviet union and the communists have enormously increased their power without hindrance.
Then there is another paragraph headed, "The neglect of Asia" in which he says:
As a result of the conflict with the Soviet union, American foreign policy has become primarily a policy for Europe, and the heart of European policy is Germany. Thus one effect of Russian pressure on the United States has been neglect of other parts of the world, notably the Far East and Latin America. As the Chinese communist armies steadily

advanced during the late months of 1948 and the early months of 1949 towards Nanking, the Chinese nationalist capital, the Truman administration kept its attention riveted on Europe and the Atlantic, although the submission of China to a communist government implied extension of Russian influence over a great portion of the globe outside Europe.
And the attitude of the Canadian government has been very much the same, even during this session. Only about a month ago, there appeared in the press dispatches to the effect that there was to be a conference in Singapore attended by high diplomatic and military planners of various nations of the commonwealth. That dispatch, however, did not mention Canada.
On October 17, on the orders of the day, 1 asked a question which is to be found at page 825 of Hansard as to whether Canada had been invited to attend this conference and, if so, whether she was going to attend. The purpose of the conference was described as being to consider the threat of communism in the Orient, and to discuss the recognition of communist China. In the absence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself answered. In effect his answer was that Canada had had no official information concerning the proposed meeting. He indicated that perhaps it was just a meeting of officials on the spot, and that no invitation had been extended to Canada. I asked then whether or not the government would make inquiries concerning this conference, and would attend if invited. The Prime Minister was rather short in his reply. In effect he brushed aside the question; I thought he did not show very much interest in the conference, and did not seem to realize just how much Canada is concerned with what is happening in the Pacific area.
In his remarks yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs showed a much clearer realization of the importance of this area. At page 1837 of Hansard he pointed out that Canada borders on the Pacific ocean, and would be very foolish to try to isolate herself from the political and economic problems of Asia. Then he went on to explain to the members that one could fly from Vancouver to the Orient within a matter of a day or two, and that now there was no longer any Far East. As he put it,-
In fact in this air age the Far East is neither far nor east.
I thought this seemed to put the situation very well. Then he went on to say:
Therefore Canadians must learn to look, as they are of course learning to look, northwest to Asia.
His sense of direction was a little poor when he said "northwest", because if Canada looked northwest to Asia all she would see would be Siberia. I think in looking across

the Pacific we must look from Siberia right down to Australia and New Zealand, taking in all the nations across the Pacific. However that may have been what the minister really intended to say.
Might I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

That it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, 1939, by reducing the area taken out of payment in an eligible area when contiguous to an ineligible area; by reducing the size of an eligible area within an ineligible township and contiguous to one that is eligible; and to bring into payment any half township outside areas already established on a legal township basis but not contiguous thereto.
Prairie Farm Assistance Act
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very sorry that I am compelled by circumstances to suggest to the various opposition groups in the house that we be allowed to proceed with this resolution and the bill based upon it in a manner which is not strictly in accordance with the rules. I find it necessary to do so because of the fact that I agreed some little time ago to go to the Royal Winter fair in Toronto tomorrow, and I have just received notice today that one of the ministers of the British government and the secretary of agriculture of the United States are to head a delegation to the FAO conference in Washington. During this session I have also intimated that the bill would be submitted to the standing committee on agriculture.
In order that it may get before that committee I have discussed with the leaders of the three opposition groups the possibility of our having the bill advanced tonight through the different stages which will make it possible to have it submitted at once to the standing committee on agriculture. It would get before that committee not later than next Monday or Tuesday, whatever might be decided upon by the members of the committee. Therefore I should like to suggest that if the resolution is allowed to proceed into the committee stage I will make a statement on it, and I shall be prepared then to answer any questions in order that all information which hon. members may desire to have at the moment may be given. Then I suggest that the bill be given second reading and be then submitted to the standing committee on agriculture. If that meets with the approval of the house we can proceed in that way and get the bill before the standing committee, after which it will come back to the house and be discussed in full in committee of the whole house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBLE AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in view of the unusual procedure and the fact that I had only three copies of the bill at hand before coming into the house, one of which I have given to the acting leader of the official opposition, the other being in the hands of one or other of the other two opposition groups, I think it might be advisable for me to read the

Prairie Farm Assistance Act bill, which is very short, so that hon. members will at least have in their minds what it provides. It reads as follows:
His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
1. Section 7 of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, 1939, chapter 50 of the statutes of 1939, as enacted by section 3 of chapter 24 of the statutes of 194748, is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"7. Notwithstanding anything contained in this act
(a)	where a rectangular block of sections of land within an eligible township having an area of not less than one-sixth of the township and a side that lies along the boundary of an ineligible area is determined by the board to have an average yield of more than ten bushels of wheat per acre, such block of sections of land shall be ineligible for award;
I might explain that by saying that under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, under the conditions which prevail at the present time, no payment can be made unless there is a block of land six miles square, that is, a legal township, in which the average yield of wheat is eight bushels or less per acre. That is the basis of the present act. Then it goes on to say that, if it is eight bushels or less per acre, from eight down to four the payment is $1.50 an acre, and from four down it is $2.50 an acre, with a minimum payment of $200 from four bushels down and a maximum payment of $500. That in general is the basis of the act as it now stands.
What clause (a) says is that if there is an area within one of these townships of six sections of land, that is, six times 640 acres, that has an average yield of more than ten bushels per acre, then that particular part of the township can be taken out. In other words, where you have an average yield of ten bushels or more in a particular part of a township covering six sections or more and lying alongside an ineligible area and the average yield may be eight bushels or less over the whole township, then that part can be taken out. The next subsection of the bill provides:
(b)	where a rectangular block of sections of land within an ineligible township having an area of not less than one-sixth of the township and a side that lies along the boundary of an eligible township is determined by the board to have an average yield of eight bushels of wheat or less per acre, such block of sections of land shall be eligible for award as though it were a complete township;
The first subsection provides that where it is over ten bushels to the acre then six sections or more may be taken out. The next subsection provides that where it is eight bushels or less per acre then six sections or more can be added in. The next subsection reads:
(c)	where the board has determined that an area is eligible for award and a rectangular block of


sections of land outside such area having an area of not less than one-half a township is determined by the board to have an average yield of eight bushels of wheat or less per acre, such block of sections of land shall be eligible for award as though it were a complete township."
That provision was first asked for by the province of Manitoba, the reason being that that province has never obtained as much by way of payments under this legislation as it has paid in. The act provides that when farmers deliver grain to the elevators in the west one per cent of the value of the grain is taken and put into a fund, and, to the extent that that does not provide enough, money is taken out of the treasury of Canada in order to make the payments. On the whole the result has been that there has been about $3 paid out of the fund for every $1 put in by farmers. That is for the whole area, but in so far as Manitoba is concerned there has not been as much paid out of the fund as has been put in by the farmers. They have discussed whether or not they should be withdrawn from the act, and have decided that it would be best to remain in. From time to time they have suggested that in Manitoba there are areas affected amounting to less than a township-and the same thing prevails in other parts of the west-which are some distance removed from the large block that enters into the general provisions of the legislation, where payments should be made. So they proposed that we should put it on a half-township basis.
We have argued against that as applying to the whole of the area in the three western provinces, saying we would have to divide each township into four divisions and check in each in order to determine whether a halftownship was in or out, which would make administration costs much too high. So as an alternative we have proposed what we are suggesting now by way of amendment to the act; that we go anywhere outside a block that has been established on the basis of the complete township and then start a new area by setting up a half-township. That halftownship may be all within a legal township of six square miles, or it may be part of any one or more townships. In other words there may be eighteen sections of land some parts of which could be in any one of four townships. That which has a yield of eight bushels or less may be set up as a unit from which we start; and then we proceed as though that were a full township and build up around it by the six-section strips provided for in the other sections, or by taking out in the same way.
In a few words, that is the meaning of this amendment. The second and last section of the bill provides that the act shall be deemed to have come into force on the 1st day of

August, 1949. The reason for that is that we announced the introduction of this bill last spring, and it was assumed that it would be passed in time to take care of this year's crop. Payments are not made until December, which is still half a month away, so if this legislation is deemed to have come into effect as of August 1, 1949, it will mean that payments will be made on the basis of the 1949 crop.
In effect those are the terms of the legislation. I do not know just what information hon. members may desire before proceeding further, but if there are any questions, or if any hon. members desire to make statements, perhaps it would be better to have that done now. I can only add that I think I have sufficient information before me to answer in a brief way any questions hon. members may desire to ask, or to give a hurried reply to any statements that may be made with respect to suggested amendments other than those now proposed.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBLE AREAS
speechtext:
I think hon. members on all sides will welcome the minister's statement and the introduction of this legislation reducing the area that may be declared eligible for payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. However, the bill does not go nearly as far as I would like to see it go. The unit basis for the payment of the bonus, as I understand it, now will be reduced from a township to a half-township. While this will help remove part of the discrimination that has prevailed in the past between farmers who have had crop failures, nevertheless a good deal of discrimination will remain. And while we welcome this legislation, it should be pointed out some farmers will be denied the bonus, a bonus they would have received had this bill not been presented, since one-sixth of an eligible township may be excluded if the average yield is less than ten bushels an acre, whereas previously one-quarter could be excluded if the average yield was more than fourteen bushels an acre.
For the life of me I cannot understand why payments are not made on an individual basis; why this rectangular provision is retained. Crop failures do not often follow the shape of a rectangle. Very often you have crop failures because of the fact that a certain area missed a local rain shower; and local showers usually go in strips. The same thing applies to hail damage. If the provisions are retained with respect to the number of sections outside an eligible township that can be declared eligible, I should like to see the rectangular provision changed so that any section adjoining any other section could obtain the crop failure payments, even though only one corner might adjoin the corner of an eligible section.
Prairie Farm Assistance Act
From time to time a number of hon. members have seemed to wonder whether legislation like this should be continued. I want to point out that this act is most necessary for the protection and well-being of a million people in western Canada living within the area known as the Pallisei triangle. Under this legislation the government has accepted at least a small measure of responsibility for those people; but surely a great deal of responsibility rests upon this government, since it was responsible for the settlement of that area many years ago. I would point out, too, that surveys in that high-risk area show that over the years a great amount of wealth has been produced. For instance, a survey of sixteen municipalities around the city of Swift Current showed that between 1919 and 1941 more than $200 million of wealth was produced. While it is true that government assistance, both provincial and federal, in that area over the same period of years amounted to $25 million, still I think it was a good investment for the people of Canada, since by paying $1 to maintain people in that district the country enjoyed the benefits of production worth $12.50.
As I said before, these people are in a high-risk area. The only way you can farm efficiently there is by farming on a large scale; and in order to do that you must have a large investment in machinery. When these farmers have two or three good crops in a row they invest a large part? of their revenue in machinery, so they may farm an economic unit. Consequently after a series of crop failures as recently experienced farmers in that area face dire need.
I think it should be pointed out also that while there have been some improvements since 1939, when this legislation was passed, the liability of the government under the act has been reduced to some extent. The legislation of 1939 contained provision for the payment of $1 per acre to farmers who had yields of between eight and twelve bushels, if the price of wheat fell to less than 80 cents a bushel. For many years now wheat has been above 80 cents a bushel; we hope it will never again go to 80 cents a bushel or lower. Nevertheless, because wheat is at a higher price now than prevailed when this act was introduced the government's responsibility is somewhat lessened.
In addition I should like to point out that under the act the farmers are today contributing more than they did in 1939. The one per cent levy which was placed in that act in 1939 has remained unchanged, but in 1939 wheat was worth 50 cents per bushe'

Prairie Farm Assistance Act while today wheat is worth more than $1.50 at the local elevator. On the basis of the collections from wheat, the revenue from this act is three times as great as it was in 1939. At the same time, while the revenue to the government under this act has been increasing, the farmers' cost of production has increased at an alarming rate. I make the statement that the farmers' cost of production in western Canada is at least twice as high as it was in 1939. I could quote figures to show the increased cost of machinery, oil, lumber, wages and repairs, everything that goes into the farmers' cost of production, but I do not think that is necessary. Anyone who knows anything about farming in that part of Canada will agree that it is a moderate statement to say that farming costs have approximately doubled since that time. The payments to the farmers who are eligible under the act, however, have not been increased.
As I said a moment ago, on the basis of wheat, the collections from farmers have trebled. I can tell the house that the people in the high-risk area of Canada are not asking for handouts. When I talk to them about this act or when they discuss with me their needs for proper crop failure assistance, almost invariably they say this: "We want the payments increased, yes, and we want the benefits paid on an individual basis. We would be quite willing to pay an increased sum into the fund if in time of crop failure we would receive a sum of money sufficient to pay our expenses for one year". Farmers have told me they would not mind if the levy were increased from one per cent to two per cent or even three per cent. Some farmers in that area have actually told me they would not be averse to paying five times the levy they have been paying, if in return for the greater contribution they would receive payments much above the maximum of $2.50 per acre; payments of six dollars an acre on an individual basis.
If the government could see fit, as I think it should, to increase the benefits under this act the farmers within the high-risk area of the Palliser triangle would be happy to make increased contributions to the fund. As the minister stated, in the past one of the obstacles to improving the act has been the fact that the farmers of Manitoba have never obtained as much in benefits from the fund as they have paid into it. I do not blame them for objecting on that basis. I do not think the objection of the farmers of Manitoba should prevent the farmers of southwestern Saskatchewan or southeastern Alberta from securing a proper scheme of crop failure protection. Therefore I suggest to the minister that there should be a zoning arrangement


whereby the levies are greater in the high-risk area, the area of frequent crop failure as compared to the levies made in the areas of low risk, the area where crop failure is seldom experienced.
The announcement of the government's intention to bring in this bill was made at the session of parliament last spring. The minister did not find it possible to present the bill at that time and so I am glad to see that this bill will become effective as of August 1, 1949. In my opinion some P. F. A. A. inspectors in the southwestern part of Saskatchewan took advantage of that announcement, and went around during the election stating that if a Liberal government were returned there would be an increase in the payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. One inspector who lives not many miles from my home said to me the night before I was taking the train for Ottawa, "Well, I suppose when you get there you are going to support the proposed increase to $5 an acre under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act". I cannot say where he got that idea, but I am saying that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act inspectors went around that part of Saskatchewan before the election saying that if the government were returned the payments would be increased.
I can say without fear of contradiction that the farmers are going to be disappointed in this bill since no provision is made for increasing the benefits under the act. I know that the Minister of Agriculture has received many petitions from farmers in that area. I have received petitions from many farmers in my constituency, in particular, a petition signed by approximately 300 people in the area around the towns of Wood Mountain, Fir Mountain, Glentworth, Flintoft, Canopus and Killdeer. In that area and throughout the whole crop failure area of Saskatchewan the farmers, businessmen and local organizations are asking that the payments be increased to at least $5 per acre. They are requesting the government, if the increases cannot be made under the act, at least to declare this a year in which an emergency exists in western Canada and take some money out of the consolidated revenue fund to make increased payments to those farmers who have suffered crop failure.
In the Leader-Post of November 12, I saw an article reporting the proceedings at the Saskatchewan wheat pool convention. That article points out that the delegates from all parts of Saskatchewan, and half of the delegates represented areas in which there were excellent crops, without exception supported a resolution calling on the federal government to pay at least $5 per acre to the

farmers who have had crop failures this year. I would plead with the minister and with members on all sides of the house to support an improved Prairie Farm Assistance Act. It is not a good thing for Canada if a million people are suffering because of successive crop failures.
In the present crop failure area there are farmers that have experienced as many as six partial crop failures since 1942. An almost total crop failure this year, after that long series of partial crop failures, has resulted in thousands of farmers being financially destitute. I say that it is the duty of the parliament of Canada to guarantee the million people living within the Palliser triangle a standard of living comparable to that enjoyed by other sections of the nation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBLE AREAS
speechtext: In view of the minister's assurance that this bill is to be sent to the committee on agriculture, I see no reason for taking the time of the house at the moment. I shall reserve further questioning until the bill is sent to that committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBLE AREAS
speechtext:
After listening to the explanation of the Minister of Agriculture regarding the three proposals contained in the resolution, I may say that I think they are a definite improvement to the act. In view of the fact that this bill is going to be referred to the committee on agriculture, I intend to be brief in my remarks.
First of all, I may say that whilst these three proposals constitute an improvement to the act, they nevertheless do not go quite as far as we should like to see them go. In the first place, we should like the unit to be reduced to a smaller size than a half township; but more especially, we should like to see the minister get away from that rectangular block. I never could understand what the magic is about the rectangle. The minister seems to be exceedingly keen on rectangles. Under section 7 of the act, it used to be in squares. Now he has got it from a square to a rectangle. Why could we not have it in a circle or in a triangle or in any irregular shape? Why does he have to stick to a rectangle alone? I mean, if a piece of land is adjacent to a rectangle, why could it not be included with the rectangle? But unless it is within the confines of the rectangle, it is ruled out. It seems to me to be a peculiar provision.
Then we feel that the amount of the bonus could be increased. I think that the farmers in the drought areas have a fairly just claim in asking that the amount be increased. I realize that the P.F.A.A. is not a solution to
Prairie Farm Assistance Act drought. It was never meant to be. It is merely for the purpose of providing assistance to farmers who lost crops as a result of drought. But on the other hand, when you remember that this act was brought into force in 1939, at a time when wheat was selling at 70 cents a bushel, there seems to be some justification in asking for an increase at this time when all other costs have risen. I would not be prepared, however, to go as far as did the hon. member for Assiniboia. I think I am in a different position from the one he probably is in. I think he must reside in an area that is totally within the drought area. I reside in a constituency 75 per cent of which is in the drought area and 25 per cent of which is out. I know that the 25 per cent would object strongly to having the levy increased to 5 per cent unless it covered all forms of hazard; that is to say, if the government sought a levy of 5 per cent and made it cover all forms of hazard, then I am satisfied that the farmers all over western Canada would be prepared to have the levy raised to. 5 per cent. But they would not be prepared to have a levy of 5 per cent on the basis of the act as it is now constituted; that is, not across western Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBLE AREAS
speechtext: In the Palliser triangle?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBLE AREAS
speechtext:
Even in the Palliser triangle. What is the Palliser triangle? It goes to Calgary, and goes down to Drumheller. You have in the Palliser triangle areas of land that average 30 to 35 bushels per acre. It takes in Drumheller, Morrin, Orkney and Rowley. They figure on 35 bushels to the acre. That is in the Palliser triangle. They never had a year when they were eligible under the act for the P.F.A.A. bonus. You could only ask for a 5 per cent levy provided you covered all forms of hazard and on a crop insurance basis rather than on the basis of the P.F.A.A.
I just want to say a few words with regard to the three proposals. Let us take the first one, which amends section 7 (a) of the act. I believe many farmers at first sight might oppose that amendment because, under it, it will now be possible for the government to withdraw from the benefits of the bonus a piece of land when the area is only six sections instead of nine. But on the other hand, I believe the amendment is a good one because it will help to reduce the discrimination that exists at the present time, owing to the way that section is drafted.
I will explain what I mean. At the present time, if there are nine sections in a square, with an average yield of over 14 bushels to the acre, within a township that is eligible that block can be withdrawn from the benefits of the bonus. But what do we find

Prairie Farm Assistance Act actually happens under that section? Very often we find that there will just be six sections with a yield of perhaps 20 bushels to the acre, and therefore the department cannot take that six sections out, because it must be nine. So to that six sections they add three sections that may have a total crop failure. But the average is still above 14. Therefore, as a result of that section, very often land is taken out of the township which has already been declared eligible and yet has suffered a total crop failure. There are several instances of that having happened. I think the minister will agree that that is a rank form of discrimination against the farmer who has had a crop failure, in view of the fact that he is residing within a township that has been declared eligible.
Under the amendment that area will be reduced to six sections, and therefore should make it easier to get the six sections than the nine. But even under the amendment there still may be discrimination because now it may be possible for them to find three sections with a yield of 20 bushels to the acre, and therefore they will be able to add to it three more sections with a total crop failure and still have an average of 10. I think in that section there should be included a proviso that no land can be taken out of an eligible township that has a yield of less than 8 bushels per acre. That would do away with the discrimination. I think that proviso definitely should be included in that section. I think the minister himself will agree that there is justification for that request. I am only asking for that to be done in a township that has been declared eligible. Once a township has been declared eligible, why should any section of land be withdrawn from the benefits of the act merely in order to make it possible to take some other land out that has a high yield?
As to the second proposal, I am thoroughly in support of it, because the situation at present is really absurd. At the present time you may have a township that is eligible. Then you may have another township alongside it that is ineligible. Yet you may have six sections along the edge of the eligible township that are denied benefits under the act because there are only six sections instead of nine. I think that any land that is adjacent to an eligible block should also be made eligible.
As to the third clause, as I have already pointed out, we are much in favour of having it reduced from a township down to half a township, but we feel that the proviso that it must be in a rectangular block should be modified so that any block of sections of land contiguous to one another equal to half a township could receive the benefits of the act.

There is one question I should like to ask the minister. Is there any understanding or regulation or provision or agreement which prohibits a province from increasing the cultivated acreage of land held by them in the drought area?

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON STATEMENT OF MR. PEARSON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the few moments at my disposal before the house rose at six o'clock I had explained that it was my intention merely to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) to deal with two questions when he closed the debate. In the first place I had asked him to go further in his statement on Canadian policy in the Pacific, pointing out the seriousness of the position in that area, and also the lack of interest in Pacific problems shown by the Canadian government.
I had also asked him concerning the proposed British commonwealth conference that is to be held in Colombo, the capital of the new dominion of Ceylon, in the month of January. Apparently the purpose of this conference is to consider the question of granting recognition to the communist regime in China and also the question of a peace treaty with Japan. I do hope that the Canadian government will not hesitate to participate in this conference. I hope further that the

Secretary of State for External Affairs will go to the conference himself. Press dispatches which announced it set out that the Right Hon. Ernest Bevin would in all probability represent the United Kingdom. I suggest to the government that it will be of sufficient importance to have our own minister represent Canada. I trust further that Canada will not hesitate to participate in any future conferences concerning Pacific problems. There has been an indifference and a reluctance to participate in these problems of the Pacific, which is not in line with the importance of the questions to every person in Canada.
If I may presume to make a suggestion to the minister, in the Pacific Canada would be very wise to work closely with the other nations of the commonwealth. Of course Australia and New Zealand view these questions in much the same light as we do ourselves, and we now have the further advantage of having the new independent nations of the commonwealth, India, Pakistan and Ceylon, ready and anxious to participate in these conferences. The British commonwealth, having interests in all parts of the world, must always of necessity stand for peace. That is true in the Pacific as it is true in the Atlantic. All these nations which will be meeting in January will have as their main concern not methods of making war in the Pacific but methods of preventing war.
I hope that in the Pacific Canada will not be a camp follower of the United States. These were the words used by the minister yesterday. While co-operating to the utmost with the United States I hope Canada will not let herself be put in the position of a camp follower. There have been actions in the past by this Canadian government, in dealing with Pacific affairs, which indicated that the attitude of the government was not very far removed from that of a camp follower. Just two years ago a British commonwealth conference was held in Canberra, and Canada sent our present minister of defence. But before we took part in that conference the Canadian government had the Canadian minister in Washington go to the department of the Secretary of State of the United States. I hold in my hand a press dispatch of July 28, 1947. The heading is: "Canada Assures U.S. No Jap Treaty 'Bloc' ". It tells of Mr. Hume Wrong, the Canadian ambassador, having gone to Mr. Norman Armour, the assistant secretary of state of the United States, telling him among other things:
I told Mr. Armour, what X am sure he already knew, that this conference does not and could not mean the formation of a common British front at the peace conference.
External Affairs
Then the present minister of defence, when he went to Canberra, made a speech; and, as he often does, he distributed copies of that speech to hon. members. I hold in my hand a copy of that speech. It was made on August 26, 1947. He took much the same line as had been taken by Mr. Hume Wrong in Washington. He said:
The conference should be useful in giving us an opportunity to exchange views in a free and noncommittal way. I daresay that no one here is in a position, even if he so desired, to commit his government to a course of action until an opportunity had been given to hear the views of other nations with interests in the Pacific.
It is very interesting to read the opinion of the Right Hon. Vincent Massey with regard to the attitude of the Canadian government at that time. As hon. members know, Mr. Massey has been both high commissioner to London and ambassador to the United States. He is our most experienced diplomat. I hold in my hand Mr. Massey's book entitled: "On being Canadian". At page 105 we find these words. He is dealing with Canada and the other nations of the British commonwealth reaching agreement on various questions. He said:
At all times we should refuse to accept the notion that there is any impropriety in our consulting together on any matter of common concern. When it was reported in the press in 1947 that we had assured the United States government that the forthcoming commonwealth conference on the peace treaty with Japan did not foreshadow the formation of a British "common front," these representations seemed both unnecessary and undignified.
I hope that there will be no such nonsense in connection with the conference at Colombo in January, and that the Canadian government will not feel that it must first go to the United States government and explain that no agreement will be reached at Colombo and therefore that the United States need not worry.
I would ask the minister, when he closes the debate, to state whether Canada is to be represented at this conference at Colombo, and also to tell us whether the government is in favour of a Pacific pact, similar to the North Atlantic treaty. He should tell us, also, where Canada stands in relation to Japan. Is it the belief of the Canadian government that the old imperial regime of Japan should be restored to power, or will the Canadian government insist that in Japan there be set up and maintained a democratic type of government?
Further, will the minister let us know whether the government has any proposals for reopening trade with China. Trade with that country is of vital importance to Canada, not only to Canadians on the Pacific coast but to Canadians from coast to coast. When the Canadian ambassador to China, the Hon. T. C.

External Affairs
Davis, returned a few weeks ago, he made a statement to the press. I have here a clipping from a Vancouver paper dated October 17, just a month ago today, under the heading "Canada-China Trade Could Re-open-Davis". The first paragraph states:
Recognition of communist China by the Canadian government is all that is needed to re-open trade between the two countries, T. C. Davis said here today.	:
We were told that Mr. Davis would be consulted upon his return and that the House of Commons would be told of the policy the Canadian government intended to adopt. Mr. Davis has now been back a month. Perhaps the minister will be in a position to go further tonight in telling us Canada's attitude toward recognition of communist China. To sum up on this first question, the time has come for Canada to take a leading part in Pacific affairs, just as she is taking in affairs of the Atlantic. I hope that will be the policy of the government.
The second question which concerns me and with which I would ask the minister to deal has to do with what one might call the continental front. Canada has an Atlantic front and a Pacific front; and we also have a continental front-or, in this case, it is in reality an Arctic front. What is the Canadian government's policy concerning the northwest portion of this continent on which we live?-and I emphasize the particular direction I have mentioned. I have in mind particularly Alaska, Yukon, the Mackenzie river basin, northern British Columbia and northern Alberta. It is time the government of Canada had a policy with regard to this area.
The United States is Alaska-conscious. In the last war the Americans had the experience of the Japanese seizing some of the islands which form part of Alaska, particularly the island of Kiska. Had it not been for a ruse on the part of the American navy and American airmen I am told Japan would have seized the next fortified base in the Aleutian chain. Now the Americans are in the position of having a potential enemy a great deal nearer Alaska than the Japanese were. Russia of course is just across Bering strait, only a few miles away from Alaska. During the war thousands of aircraft were flown from the United States to Edmonton, across the Yukon, Alaska and Bering strait to Siberia. Quite properly, the Americans are greatly concerned about Alaska and about the whole northwestern portion of this continent.
Within the last few weeks a measure has come before congress giving the President

power to negotiate with Canada for the survey of a railway line from Prince George in central British Columbia, up through the Yukon to connect with the Alaska railway. This has happened while the house has been in session.
A press dispatch before me from Washington dated October 4 bears the heading "U.S. Senate Committee Backs B.C. Rail Link", and states:
A move to merge the Alaskan railroad with the United States and Canadian railway systems moved: another step forward in congress today.
Then it goes on to describe what has been said about that bill. On October 26 President Truman signed the bill, which is described as one authorizing him to undertake an agreement with Canada which might lead to the construction of a 1,400-mile railway to connect Alaska with the American northwest. That, of course, should be of interest to the Canadian government. Certainly it is of the utmost interest to the people of western Canada. We are directly involved in this proposal. Yet our government seems to be holding back, and does not seem to be greatly interested.
Earlier in the session I asked this question:
Have there been any negotiations between the government of Canada and the government of the United States concerning the construction of a railway through Canada to Alaska?
The answer was:
There have been no formal negotiations, but informal discussions took place in September and October, 1942.
Although that question was asked while the United States was in process of passing the bill, apparently the government of Canada had had no discussion for seven years. My second question was:
Have any surveys been made or authorized by the Canadian government in connection with such a railway?
To which the answer was:
Yes, the Canadian government authorized the United States army engineers to make a survey in 1942.
Then about the middle of October we find this dispatch headed "U.S.-Alaska Railway-Far Off in Future." The article was written by Mr. Hardy, one of the senior members of the press gallery. The first paragraph of his article states:
Although the United States congress has voted funds to cover the cost of a survey for a railway route which would link the U.S. and Alaska through Canada, government officials here expressed the view-
And he refers to Ottawa-
-that it might be years before such a survey gets-underway.

The final paragraph states:
Officials of the Department of External Affairs said that in any event negotiations in connection with the suggested survey would take "a long period of time."
J udged by government standards that might mean a good many years.
On November 4 when we were discussing the bill to provide a subsidy to the Pacific Great Eastern Railway I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) about this matter. His answer is found as follows at page 1461 of Hansard:
As to the second question, with regard to the proposal of the United States, I understand that the bill to which my hon. friend referred has been passed by congress. Until representations are made on the official level by the United States government to the Canadian government, it is impossible to consider the question of a survey such as my hon. friend suggests.
Then I asked:
Would Canada participate in a survey?
The Minister of Transport replied:
I think the answer would depend on whether or not we are invited to participate. At the moment I am not aware that we have been invited. When we are invited, I presume we shall look at the position then.
It hardly befits a grown-up nation, such as Canada now is, to be so coy about suggestions of this kind. I submit that the Canadian government should have views on this matter, and should be in a position to disclose them to the Canadian parliament, and in that way to the Canadian people. Yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) said that the St. Lawrence waterway should be developed. He rapped the United States over the knuckles for being so slow about making a move with regard to the St. Lawrence waterway. Perhaps we could help them to make up their minds if we offered to co-operate in connection with the railway to Alaska, which would not only benefit Alaska but would also be of great benefit to Canada. I do not doubt that they are just as anxious for us to make up our minds as to what we propose to do about the northwestern part of the continent as we are to have them make up their minds about the St. Lawrence waterway. I suggest there is great need now for a clear-cut Canadian policy for the Pacific northwestern area. I ask the minister to explain to us this evening the stand which the Canadian government takes on this question as well as the question which I dealt with earlier in my remarks.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON STATEMENT OF MR. PEARSON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to commend the minister for the comprehensive review of current events in all parts of the world that he has presented to the house. Comments
External Affairs
from all sides of the house were so favourable that I think the conclusion is quite obvious that I can very well dispense with adding anything further. I am fully aware that the house is anxious to conclude this debate tonight, and I assure you that I will cut my remarks down to the minimum and not delay the house unduly.
It has been my privilege to represent Canada at the fourth session of the general assembly of the United Nations. Therefore, I was particularly interested this afternoon and yesterday when hon. members who had had that experience in the past gave their impressions of the organization. I was particularly impressed this morning with the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) when he said that he had been struck by the great prestige of Canada at the United Nations. I think that is the first impression anybody receives who goes to the United Nations, because it is paramount, and it is always very gratifying to a Canadian upon reaching the scene. I suppose there are many reasons for the high prestige that our country enjoys. No doubt a great deal of the credit goes to the minister himself because of his personal ability, with which most hon. members of the house are familiar. When you couple with that his many years of experience in the diplomatic field, and his very pleasant and engaging personality, then you pretty well have the reason why he enjoys so enviable a position at Lake Success, and thereby reflects credit upon Canada as a whole.
It was a tribute to his country when he was elected chairman of the political committee, the most important committee of that organization, but it was also a tribute to the man himself, because after all hon. members will realize that any man who assumes the responsibility of chairmanship of such a committee must have personal attributes to carry out that responsibility. The minister combines both the qualities necessary for leadership of the Canadian delegation and the required ability and experience to perform his duties as chairman of the political committee. Everybody is agreed in saying that he is doing a splendid job.
I also want to mention briefly that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is bringing honour to his country at Lake Success. We all know that he can speak very forcibly, and with complete honesty and frankness. I should also like to mention to the house Canada's permanent delegate at the United Nations, General Mc-Naughton. I believe he is doing a splendid

External Affairs
job in New York for Canada. I do not think that any more conscientious delegate could be found. As we all know, he is an arduous worker, and possibly one of the most active members among the delegations. I should also like to mention that on the second day after I reached Lake Success I heard echoes of the reputation of St. Laurent and Ilsley still ringing in the corridors and the committee rooms.
Lastly, I want to join with the hon. member for Winnipeg North when he said this morning that a great deal of the credit goes to the officials of the Department of External Affairs. Most of them are young, hardworking men. As a matter of fact, by the standards of other delegations they are rather underpaid, but they are not just doing a job. They are pursuing a cause, and they are completely devoted to their task. There is no question that a great deal of the credit should go to these hard-working and able men. The fortunate position that Canada finds itself in also contributes to that prestige because, as has been mentioned, Canada is expected to and does approach all questions from an objective angle.
After all, we in Canada have no special axe to grind with anybody. In the past we have had delegations who have worked most strenuously and earnestly to try to further the aims of the United Nations. They have established themselves in the minds of the members of all delegations as being most sincere. In other words, they are known as people who do their homework before they go into the committee rooms.
For all these reasons, it is most gratifying to any Canadian to see the high place that our great country enjoys in the deliberations of this world organization. I would be remiss in my duty if I did not pass on to all hon. members of the House of Commons the gratitude of the various delegations that was expressed to me as a Canadian delegate when the name of a distinguished servant of this House of Commons was submitted for nomination this year. I refer to our Auditor General, Mr. Watson Sellar. As hon. members know, he has been chairman of the board of auditors of the United Nations ever since the organization was formed, and from all accounts he has done a marvellous job. He has contributed in large measure to the streamlining of the organization, and has made it more efficient and less costly. When his term expired this year everyone seemed very anxious that he should continue at his job, and begged that his name be allowed to stand again. Rarely have I heard so much praise for the work of
[Mr. Jutras.J
an official; and this too, I think, has contributed to the high place Canada occupies in that forum.
I listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) yesterday, when they gave their impressions of various conferences they had attended. Perhaps it is because my experience is still fresh and new, but I must admit I was most favourably impressed with the possibility that the United Nations organization might maintain peace in the world, not so much as we see that organization today but rather as we may hope to see it in a few years. Of course, unlike the hon. member for Peel, I was not at San Francisco when the United Nations was born, so I am spared the feeling of more or less frustration which he seemed to experience yesterday.
In our consideration of the United Nations I think it most important to remember that it is a permanent organization. I believe we should always avoid thinking of it as an experiment. We have built this organization, which is now only being completed. As a matter of fact we now have under construction a building to house the United Nations, and there is nothing temporary about the structure now rising in Manhattan, which will cost some $65 million, I hope it will help people consider the United Nations as something permanent.
We have experienced a great many crises of ideologies since the end of the war, and we have seen many movements toward national independence in various parts of the world. If we permit ourselves to think of the organization in terms of one aspect of its work only, or if we attempt to judge it on an immediate as opposed to a long-range view, that could be almost fatal to the organization.
At this stage I think it appropriate to recall briefly the basic premises at San Francisco, as I understand them. I believe the founders of the United Nations agreed that peace could be maintained only by a universal organization based upon a universally accepted charter. They rejected anything less or anything short of that; and they included all major forces at work in all parts of the world. The view held in some quarters that the founders of the United Nations might have contemplated that it would abolish all differences of interest and ideology is, I submit, a fallacy. I do not believe the founders of the United Nations ever contemplated that this organization would end differences of interest or ideology. They never contemplated that the great powers

would always act together in unity and brotherhood. No doubt they hoped and wished for that, but it was not necessarily one of the premises upon which the organization was founded. They did reject the concept that differences could be settled only on the battlefield, and agreed to keep those differences, ideological or otherwise, within peaceful bounds. That, I believe, is the aim and object of the United Nations. So far, I submit, the organization has done that to a marked degree. It is true that it has not succeeded in abolishing the fear of war, but I submit that it certainly has lessened that fear. It has also removed obstacles on the road to a peaceful world.
It was my privilege to represent Canada on the second and fifth committees. I do not wish to take time to explain everything the fifth committee did, but it is the committee that considers financial and administrative matters. Dealing with figures may sound rather dull, but there were certain compensating features. Since most resolutions involving the expenditure of money had to be referred to that committee, we dealt with most of the resolutions that came up for consideration in the other committees. To a newcomer like myself, that provided an opportunity of obtaining a more or less general picture of all the activities of the organization.
Too many people think of the United Nations in terms of the general assembly alone. I know I fell into that error at one time. But after all the general assembly is like our parliament here. When the session is prorogued, the work of parliament goes on. So it is at the United Nations; from the general assembly branch out all the commissions that carry out the policy that has been laid down. So I would recommend that all hon. members read the budget of the United Nations, in order to get a general picture of the activities of that organization. As I said, matters of policy are laid down by the general assembly; then commissions of inquiry are sent to various parts of the world to help nations that have problems and do not know how to solve them. These commissions find the source of the trouble and advise how it may be overcome.
Then there are what I consider to be the most successful of all, the political commissions of conciliation that are to be found in all the troubled parts of the world. They are sent out to try to bring a conflict to an end, or to offer solutions, or to prevent conflicts from arising, and in spite of certain
External Affairs
failures I believe they have been very successful so far. The world has every reason to be gratified at the success so far.
We listened to an interesting speech delivered by the member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. MacKenzie), who told us of his experience in China. He emphasized the humanitarian efforts of the United Nations. This gives the members of the house an idea of the efforts of the United Nations in China, and the story of those efforts could be duplicated in many other countries if time permitted.
When we are considering the achievements of the United Nations, I should like to mention two or three. The resolving of the crisis with regard to Berlin has probably gone by with too little notice. Everyone will recall the tension that existed in the world when the four great powers reached a deadlock last year. I remember quite well the feeling of impending disaster which permeated the world. The newspapers were full of gloom. The question was brought before the security council in September of last year. At that time many people feared this question would break the United Nations. Conciliating forces were set in motion, however, and a committee of currency experts set out to break the deadlock by introducing a single currency into Berlin. This did not bring immediate results, but it certainly eased the tension. It reduced the threat of war and gave us the time to set other factors in motion. This resulted in the resumption of negotiations by the great powers after seventeen months of complete stalemate. I believe that the results achieved in this instance alone should make us grateful to the United Nations Organization.
I need not recall the Palestine question to which the minister referred. I believe everyone is quite familiar with it. The creation of a state in Palestine was probably one of the epic events of history, which was achieved without a major war. Then there is the example of Kashmir where a United Nations commission has known great success. Four hundred million people were involved, and they were spared the worst disaster of all, religious warfare.
In Indonesia the United Nations played a decisive part in the effort to secure a peaceful settlement of that dispute, and to secure a peaceful transition to national independence for 70 million Indonesians. More people live in those countries than in all of Europe. This gives one an idea of the importance of these efforts of the United Nations. We must remember that these achievements were accomplished without the aid of any military

External Affairs
forces whatever, because the United Nations does not possess any military forces as yet. It was merely the moral influence of the organization that asserted itself in the various parts of the world.
Is it unreasonable, Mr. Speaker, to believe that if the moral influence of this organization were allowed to assert itself for a few years more it could continue to help the world secure peace? In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say it is apparent that the United Nations Organization will serve us only to the extent that we put our faith in it and remain with it through thick and thin.
